2047.title: The word "district" itself
2047.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token: the word "district" or "District", in any sense. It is strongest when the word closes a place or institution name at the start of an encyclopedia article (an Indian or Turkish administrative district, a US school district, a magisterial district, the District of Columbia), and somewhat weaker for "district attorney" and "red-light district" in plot summaries. Other words for areas or offices (county, province, region, attorney, school) do not fire it without the word "district".

3225.title: The letter pair "ow" inside a word
3225.explanation: This unit reacts to the marked token itself: a word piece spelled "ow" (or a piece containing it, such as " Bow", " Dow", " Chow", "vow", "owed"), almost always in the middle or at the end of a longer word. Most of the strongest cases are surnames and other names split into pieces (Rogow, Dashow, Dowd, Plowman, Popow, Doctorow, Lubow, Leonowens, Kowalski, Bowfinger, Chowdhury), with a few ordinary words (Meow, Avowal, Advowson, Endowments, stowaway, vow). The meaning of the surrounding text does not matter; it is a spelling detector, and it does not fire on the same sound spelled differently or on names without the "ow" piece.

5762.title: Last piece of a fantasy franchise name
5762.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a famous made-up name from fantasy, horror or genre fiction: "busters" in Ghostbusters, "-earth" in Middle-earth, "Rings" in The Lord of the Rings, "illion" in Silmarillion, "smouth" in Innsmouth, "Lantern" in Green Lantern, "Rangers" in Power Rangers, "andre" in Melisandre. It reacts to the marked word piece itself once the earlier piece has made the name recognisable (Tolkien, Lovecraft, Ghostbusters and superhero titles dominate), not to the plot around it. The same pieces in ordinary use (a ring, a lantern, park rangers, the earth) and the first half of such names are not what it marks; a few weaker cases are simply the tail of an exotic proper name (Kadesh, a Chinese transliteration of Orodreth).

6972.title: The word-piece "Know", especially capitalised
6972.explanation: Fires on the token itself: the word-start piece ' Know' with a capital K, wherever it appears, whether as the first piece of a surname (Knowles, Knowby, Knowland), in a title or proper name (Know-Nothing, I Still Know What You Did Last Summer, U Know What I'm Sayin?, KnowItAll, Mr. Know It All) or otherwise. It fires more weakly on the lower-case forms know, knows, knew and the 'know' inside 'Unknowing'. The meaning of the surrounding text does not matter, and words about knowledge that are spelled differently (aware, learns, realizes) do not trigger it.

10540.title: Grab-bag of specific rare tokens (塾, metavar, Lauderdale, Gotham)
10540.explanation: This first-layer unit reacts to the marked token itself, not to the meaning of the text before it. It fires on a small, unrelated set of particular tokens: the character 塾 (private school / cram school, in Chinese and Japanese text such as 義塾, 家塾, 植芝塾), the argparse/optparse keyword " metavar" in Python code, the place name "Lauderdale" (Fort Lauderdale), the rare characters 喰 and 筅 (茶筅, tea whisk), and the words "Fellowship" and "centerpiece"; in the plot summaries it fires more weakly (about 0.6) on the word "Gotham" wherever it occurs. There is no shared idea linking these tokens, and other school words, other argparse keywords (dest, default, help) or other city names do not trigger it.

38348.title: Possessive 's after a year, institution or place
38348.explanation: The unit fires on the possessive ending ('s, or a bare ' after a word ending in s) when it is attached to a year, an organisation, a broadcaster, a school or a place that is being used as a label for what follows, usually a titled work or a named thing: "1989's Trouble Walkin'", "NYU's Tisch Drama Program", "CBS' 60 Minutes", "NPR's Anne Powers", "Philadelphia's Institute of Contemporary Art". It is reacting to the marked token itself in that grammatical setting, and is strongest for the journalistic "year's + title" construction common in music and film writing. It fires more weakly on ordinary possessives of companies, places or ships (Suntory's, Iran's, Harvard's, Discovery's), and it does not fire on apostrophes inside foreign names or transliterations (l'Arche, Vasyl'), which belong to the opposite pole.

45473.title: The word "villain" and its equivalents
45473.explanation: Fires on the word "villain" itself, in any form and at whichever piece completes it: "Anti-Villain League", "Villains United", "arch-villain", "supervillain", "villainous", "Best Villain", even the misspelling "villianous". It fires in the same way on the Chinese word for a villain role (反派, peaking on 派) and, a little less, on "antagonist" in phrases such as "the main antagonist". It is a reaction to the word that labels someone the bad guy of a story, not to wicked deeds: a criminal or killer described without that label does not trigger it, and the French look-alike "Vilain" (ugly) fires only on spelling.

53703.title: The name "Bruce"
53703.explanation: The unit fires on the token of the name Bruce itself, whoever bears it and whether it is a first, middle or last name: Robert the Bruce and King Robert Bruce of Scotland, Robert Bruce Banner (the Hulk), Bruce Wayne, Blanche Bruce, Joseph Bruce Ismay, narrator Robert C. Bruce. It also fires when the name is split into pieces or written in another script ("Bru-ce", "Bruces", Korean 브루스). It is a reaction to the word, not to the surrounding story; other names in the same sentences (Robert, Wayne, Banner, Batman) do not set it off.

64864.title: Name stops short of its earlier longer form
64864.explanation: Fires on the token right after a name or number that is a shortened version (a prefix) of a longer one seen earlier in the same document, i.e. where the earlier string went on but this one ends. In code: "for block in" after many "for blockNumber in", "is_file(obj" after "is_file_location(obj)", "renderHttpAsJson($" after "renderHttpAsJsonApi($error)", "int(x)]" after "int(xpos)]", "request)," after "request_info),", "URI_TPL_HTTP]." after "URI_TPL_HTTP_AUTH]", "Session(SessionData" after "SessionData(dict)". In prose and tables the same thing happens with numbers: "169.1 mph" after "169.173 mph", "1 Train" after "1006 Train", "+1000 (" after "+10000 (", "15 n." after "153 n.". The peak token itself is just whatever comes next (a bracket, "in", a space, "||"); an exact repeat of the earlier name, or a bracket after a name with no longer sibling, does not trigger it. In plot summaries it is only faintly active, on the word after a shortened name such as "Bruce" after "Bruce Wayne" or "Don Diego" after "Don Diego Vega".

65790.title: Game-rules text: mechanics words like "knock out"
65790.explanation: The unit fires inside descriptions of how a game is played (video-game "Gameplay" sections and tabletop role-playing rulebooks), on a content word that names a game mechanic or game element. The clearest case is "knock" in "knock opponents out / off the screen / off-course" (four of the top passages), followed by similar mechanic words: items "dropped" by monsters, players who "drop" in, "trapping" a ghost, hit points "recovered", "secondary" skills, a "ritual" spell, "Soul" Tethers, "Trickster" Gods, element"als". What matters is the surrounding game-rules context rather than any single word, so the peak token varies; in ordinary film plot summaries the unit is weak (0.4 or less) and lands on unrelated words (neon, antimatter, true, Florence) with no shared pattern.

70156.title: Plain nouns as technical compound heads
70156.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked word itself: a short everyday noun used in a technical sense as the last word of a compound, most often "bath" (oil bath, acid bath, water bath, electroplating bath), "feed/feeds" (video feeds, alerts and feeds, high-definition feed) and "washes" (coloured washes, thin washes), plus "archive", tar-"ball", organ "beds" and L-"uts". In the plot summaries the same shape appears much more weakly on "energy field", "War Rig", "warning beacon" and "prison" enclosure. It is a word-level unit rather than a topic: the contexts range over metalworking, chemistry, painting, broadcasting and software. It does not appear to fire on these words in their ordinary sense (taking a bath, feeding someone) or on the modifier that comes before them.

71327.title: Safe, will, check: things that hold money
71327.explanation: The unit fires on the noun itself when it names an object that holds or carries money or an inheritance: above all a safe or safes (opened, cracked, hidden in a wall, full of cash or bullion), and also a will (the testament), a check, a bank's till, and more weakly an envelope or trunk with something hidden in it. The surrounding text is nearly always a robbery, heist, bank or inheritance story, which tells the model that "safe", "will" and "check" are meant as these things. The same spellings in other senses fire much more weakly (a "safe house", a "safe place" reach only about half to two thirds), and the verb uses of "will" and "check" do not appear among the strong passages.

71825.title: The word "therapy" (psychological treatment)
71825.explanation: The unit fires on the token "therapy" itself, almost always meaning talk therapy or counselling for a mental or emotional problem: someone attends therapy, is in therapy, underwent therapy, or deals with trauma, addiction or a troubled relationship through therapy. It is reacting to the word, not predicting it, and the surrounding context (psychiatrist, sessions, addiction, depression, self-esteem) only raises the strength a little. Related forms and medical senses fire much more weakly ("shock therapy", "therapies", "therapeutic properties"), and mental-health text that does not contain the word (for example passages about body image, depression or anxiety alone) does not fire it.

73576.title: Chinese "belongs to" plus game and merchandise jargon
73576.explanation: The unit reacts to particular tokens rather than to a scene, and they fall into two groups with no single clear idea joining them. One is the Chinese character 屬/属 in 屬於/属于 ("belongs to"), 專屬 ("exclusive") and 所屬 ("affiliated with"), plus 具 in 道具 ("props/items"). The other is English video-game and fan-culture vocabulary: loot, kit, unlocks/unlocked, balance (patch), toxic (behaviour) and merch/merchandise/merchandising. A loose link may be things that are owned, acquired or belong to someone, but that is a guess; in ordinary plot summaries it fires only weakly (about 0.3) on "toxic" and on unrelated word-pieces such as "sous", "erst" and the "ore" of Commodore.

74990.title: Second predicate attached to a noun without a link word
74990.explanation: This is a grammar unit, not a topic unit. It fires on the word that starts a new verb, participle or manner adverb directly after a noun phrase that has just served as the object or complement of an earlier verb, with no linking word such as who, that or and: "It was you fell over me", "It was my brother got the knowledge", "it is this unhappy passion disturbs her", "a family consists of", "identifies Napier killed his parents", "has Michael live", "a remark dropped by", "coats hung up", "seized the volume rapturously". In code the same shape appears as a chained call or operator right after a completed expression (".append(...).append", "push(n +="). It does not fire on a verb that follows its subject in an ordinary simple clause, or where a relative pronoun or conjunction is present; the weaker passages (adverbs after an object, reduced participles) are looser versions of the same shape.

76609.title: "Released as / based on" links describing a work
76609.explanation: It fires in encyclopedia-style descriptions of a film, game, song, book or TV series, on the linking word that ties the work to its form, source or role: "released as", "is based on", "loosely based on", "adapted from", "serves as / serving as" (a prequel, sequel, epilogue), "started as", "originally known as", "dedicated to", "opens and ends with", and in plot summaries "produced by", "makes references", "ends with", "closing text". The unit reacts to the meta-level framing of a work (what it is, what it derives from, how it is packaged) rather than to events inside a story, and it peaks on the connecting word itself (as, based, adapted, with). Ordinary uses of "as" or "based" outside a description of a creative work do not trigger it, and release dates or "in theaters" phrases belong to the opposite pole; one strong passage (a list of "Singha" golf tournaments) does not fit.

86683.title: Token right after "the" plus a proper name
86683.explanation: The unit fires on the small word, suffix or punctuation mark that comes straight after a proper name which was itself introduced by "the": "the Ipswich« to» Shotley road", "the Castleford« and» Melford properties", "the Highlandtown«'s»", "The Docker«'s» Guild", "the Windows« is»", "the Montreal« on»", "the Paganism«,»". It is reacting to the preceding context (article + name, often a place or surname that does not normally take "the", or a name used as a modifier), not to the marked word itself, which varies (and, to, 's, in, is, was, a comma). In the plot summaries the same shape appears more weakly as "the Phantasm, a", "The Tulku, a", "the Overlook's", "the Parks'", "the Hermes,". A plain "and the" or a name without a preceding "the" does not trigger it (the opposite pole takes "X and the").

109416.title: Acting for attention, fame or personal gain
109416.explanation: The unit fires when the text names a self-serving motive behind someone's behaviour: doing something for attention, publicity, notoriety, glory, to impress someone, to look good, or for money and personal gain. The peak lands on the word that states the motive ("seeking attention", "publicity-seeking", "for the sake of gain", "commercial gain", "easy buck", "just to impress her", "desire for notoriety", the Chinese idiom for fishing for fame), so it is reacting to the meaning of the phrase rather than to one spelling. It is strongest when the motive is an accusation or dismissal (he made it up for attention, it was only a publicity stunt), and it does not fire on neutral uses of words like attention or gain that carry no sense of ulterior motive.

109519.title: Head-to-head link: one side beats another
109519.explanation: The unit fires on the word that sets one named side against a counterpart of the same kind, most strongly the result verb in a match-up: "Chicago beat Kansas City", "Mexico beat Uruguay", "which beats Mi'll's", "Adamson def. UST", "#27 vs #24", "he can beat the card". It reacts to the meaning of the text so far (a first competitor has just been named and a pairwise contest or pairing is being stated), not to one spelling, since it also fires on rock-paper-scissors options and a rival falling for the same woman. A weaker, looser group is any item being tied to its partner item: passes it to his neighbor, link it to its dependency, this.parent, the pole of another magnet, the second beam splitter. It does not fire on teams or games merely being mentioned, on standings or scores without an "A beat B" pairing, or on the opposite pole's material (abstract descriptions of graphs, networks and models).

112000.title: Names inside wrestling, fight-sport and superhero texts
112000.explanation: The unit reacts to the kind of text it is in: articles about professional wrestling and lucha libre, kickboxing and MMA careers, and superhero comics or their plots. Within such text it peaks on a piece of a stage name, alias, team, promotion or event name (Matt-ias Wilde, Hector Gar-za, All-Star, Justice League, Phantom Lady, Lock-down, Steel, Dare-devil, King-pin, Night-wing, Red Hood), and sometimes on a nearby word such as 'the' before a promotion or 'mixed' rules. The token itself matters little; the same words or name fragments in ordinary prose, sport without fighters or stories without costumed characters do not fire it.

112625.title: Superhero comics names, titles, powers and gear
112625.explanation: Most firings are inside text about American superhero comics (DC and Marvel): on character names and codenames (Remy LeBeau/Gambit, Northstar, Ariel, Kent, Robin, Bat-Family), on comic titles and issue markers ("Action" Comics, the "#" in "Green Arrow (vol. 3) #27", pinups), and on stock superhero powers and equipment ("the ability to fly", costume, mask, grapple, grappling hook). It reacts to the surrounding superhero-comics setting rather than to one word, so the same words in an ordinary context should not trigger it, and mythological or manga fantasy figures (nine-tailed fox, Loki, Naruto) belong to the opposite pole. A second, separate group at the very top is theoretical physics: "supersymmetry transformations" and "variation" in field-theory articles (supergravity, source field, thermal quantum field theory); this may be linked only through "super-" vocabulary, and I cannot tie it firmly to the comics group.

114423.title: Computer hacking: "hacks into", hacker
114423.explanation: The unit fires when someone breaks into a computer system: it peaks on "hack", "hacks", "hacking", "hacker", and most often on the "into" right after "hacks" (hacks into the CCTV system, a satellite, a database, someone's computer). It also fires on closely related wording such as "access computer files" and on the name of a team's tech expert (Tej in the Fast & Furious plots). Much more weakly it responds to technology-and-gadget characters and devices (Stark, Rhodes, the Batwing, a grappling hook). The word "into" after other verbs, such as physically breaking into a house or a building, does not produce the peak.

116209.title: First piece of a predictable name or term
116209.explanation: No single topic; the unit fires on the opening piece of a name or fixed term whose continuation is nearly certain, usually right after a phrase that sets it up. The clearest group is a first name given after a role: "his butler, Alfred" (Pennyworth), "Special Agents Sam" (Hanna), "James" (Gordon), "the Guardians" (of the Universe), "Warden"-turned-Mayor, and likewise "red" (supergiant), "National Center", "Edict" (of Toleration). A second group is the word that opens the defining part of an encyclopedia first sentence ("in which the lifter", "where the polypeptide chain", "for associating", "by rolling"), and a third is the middle of a technical word or code token (Accretion, Layered, infrared, 12-degree, '-t'). It does not fire on the surname or the end of the term, and the opposite pole takes the final piece of surnames (Westcott, Libby, Appleby).

122592.title: Characters and scenes inside famous stories
122592.explanation: The unit fires when the text points to a specific character, place or moment inside a well-known work of fiction, mostly classic novels and plays and some famous films: Heathcliff in Wuthering Heights, Myrtle Wilson in The Great Gatsby, Fantine in Les Miserables, Gateshead in Jane Eyre, Wickham, Bennet and Netherfield in Pride and Prejudice, Kinderman in The Exorcist, Corleone in The Godfather. It peaks on the piece of the name that makes it recognisable (Heath, ine, ham, field, head) or, in a second related group, on the word that opens a reference to something within the work ("In the book, the mockingbird", "at the play-scene", "Colonel Graff states", "when Andy first arrives", "repeated several times in the movie"). It reacts to the meaning of the context, a famous story being retold or discussed, and not to one word; names of people outside a story, such as actors and authors, and character names in obscure plots fire much less.

124334.title: Names of comic-book villains, chiefly Lex Luthor
124334.explanation: It fires on the name token of a well-known supporting character or villain from superhero comics, in text that is already about DC or Marvel stories. By far the most common trigger is 'Lex' in Lex Luthor or LexCorp (also 'uthor' in President Luthor); the rest are the same kind of name: Norman Osborn, J. Jonah Jameson, Lucy Lane, Jor-El, Ronan the Accuser, the Sinestro Corps, an AIM agent, and more weakly Thomas Wayne and Scarecrow. It reacts to the name itself, not to what follows, and it favours the antagonist or side character over the hero: Superman, Batman and Spider-Man themselves are not at the peaks. One weaker firing on 'in' just before 'Jason Todd' does not fit the token pattern but stays in the same setting.

127178.title: Names and titles in film and comics credits
127178.explanation: The unit fires inside credit-style text about films, television, games and comics, on the first or middle piece of a multi-part name or fixed title whose remainder is predictable. One group is personal and character names in cast lists and credits (Am-ara Aquilla, Din-ah Laurel Lance, Scott Lobdell, Scott Porter, Rid-ley Scott, Frances Lawrence, St-ana Katic, Richard Roe-per, Bruce, Superman, Night-wing); a second group is the word "executive" just before "producer(s)" or "produced", plus similar fixed labels such as "N-andi Awards" and "Vol." before an issue number. It does not fire on ordinary narrative words or on names in non-entertainment contexts; it needs the cast, crew or credits setting.

127524.title: Theatre and stage plays as a medium
127524.explanation: The unit fires on the word that names stage theatre or a play as a kind of performance: "theater", "plays", "play", "stage", "drama", and the same idea in Arabic ("مسرحيات", plays) and French ("théâtrale"). It is strongest in biographies of actors and directors and in film-crew articles, where theatre is listed beside film and television or opens a "Theater" section; the verb "play" (to play a role) also triggers it. More weakly it fires on other words for a medium, format or part of a work ("live-action", "video", "production", "game", "scene", "epilogue", "scenario"). It does not fire on fight scenes, stunts or choreography, which belong to the opposite pole, nor on film titles and cast lists as such.

130069.title: DC Comics names: Superman, Krypton, Arrow
130069.explanation: The unit fires on the token of a name that belongs to the DC Comics world, most strongly the Superman family and the Arrow television franchise: "Arrow" in "Arrowverse" and the series Arrow, "Clark" in Clark Kent, "El" in Kal-El and Kon-El, and "rypton" in kryptonite and Kryptonian, with weaker firing on other DC names such as J'onn J'onzz and Jay Garrick. It reacts to the marked name itself, read in a superhero context, not to the surrounding plot. Names from the rival Marvel world (Thanos, the Avengers, X-Men) do not fire it; they drive the opposite pole, and ordinary uses of words like "arrow" or "Clark" outside this setting are not among its passages.

131610.title: Flash and Fantastic Four character names completed
131610.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself when it completes a well-known comic-book name, above all from the Flash family (Barry Allen, The Flash, Central City, Jay Garrick / Flash, Martin Stein) and the Fantastic Four (Reed Richards, Johnny Storm, Mister Fantastic). It is driven by the name string rather than the scene: it fires on "Barry Allen" even when it is a con man's alias or a wrestler's ring name, on "Central City" in a Fantastic Four plot, and weakly on "Flash" inside "Flashbacks". In the plot summaries it fires more weakly on other superhero-world names and words such as Barbara (Gordon), Murdock and secret "identity". Ordinary personal names and place names outside these comic-book characters do not trigger it.

132337.title: Stan Lee and Marvel Comics creator credits
132337.explanation: The unit fires most strongly on "Lee" in the name "Stan Lee", almost always inside the stock opening of a Marvel Comics character article ("appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics. Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby"). A weaker second group is the word "created" in the same credit line for other Marvel creators, and a third, weaker still, is the names of Marvel characters and their supporting cast, mainly from Daredevil (Murdock, Elektra, Fisk, Daredevil) plus "the Penguin" and Jonah Jameson "the publisher". It is reacting to the marked token as a Marvel-comics name or credit word; the opposite pole takes DC and crossover-event titles (Black Lantern, Blackest Night, Sinestro, Civil War), and a Lee or a "created by" outside comic-book text should not fire it.

132685.title: Authorities putting down a rebellion or crime
132685.explanation: The unit fires on the words that say a ruler, army or police force is forcibly suppressing opposition: above all "down" in "put down / putting down the rebellion, uprising, insurrection, revolt", and likewise "crack" / "cracking" (down), "crackdown", "crush a rebellion", "fighting organized crime" and the Chinese word for encircling and wiping out rebels. It reacts to the meaning of the phrase (the stronger side stamping out rebels, hostile groups or criminals), with the peak on the suppression verb or its particle. In the plot summaries the weaker firings are the law-enforcement relatives of this idea: "cracking down on corruption", "war on crime", "district attorney", "apprehending", "in pursuit", "sent after him". It does not appear to respond to "down" as a plain direction or to fighting between equals in an ordinary battle; what matters is suppression of a revolt or of crime by those in power.

135688.title: Two-Face, Flash names and paired maths terms
135688.explanation: No single idea covers the strongest passages; they fall into two loosely related groups. One group is the last token of a comic-book character's name or alias, above all "Two-Face" (peak on "ace", which accounts for every plot-summary firing), and also "the Flash", "Flashpoint", "Hal Jordan" and "Yellowjacket". The other group is a technical term naming a kind or part in mathematics, physics or software: the "symmetric" part of a tensor, "alternating" polynomials, the "double cover" of a group, a "dynamic" binding, an "interface" type, assembled in "code". A possible thread is two-sidedness (symmetric versus antisymmetric, even versus odd, double, Two-Face), but several firings (a taxon name, a Bible verse number, a voice actor's surname) do not fit it, and ordinary character names or ordinary uses of words like "face" do not appear among the firings.

136830.title: "English" language, "No Limit", fixed compound terms
136830.explanation: The strongest firings fall into three related groups rather than one clean idea. The largest is the word "English" used for the language ("English-language newspaper", "in the English language", "speaks English, French", "use of English as medium of instruction"); the second is "Limit" in the poker term "No Limit Hold'em"; the third is a piece of a fixed, usually hyphenated technical compound or set name ("Strongly NP-complete", "Problem-Oriented Policing", "Anti-Semitism", "Wigner-Yanase-Dyson", "t-norm", "strategic choice"). What they share is that the marked token sits inside a stock multi-word label whose next part is predictable; the weaker plot-summary firings ("Bruce Wayne", "Dynamic Duo", "expert in martial arts", "tactical support") fit that loosely. It does not fire on "English" as a nationality ("an English professional poker player") or on ordinary free word combinations.

144750.title: Airmen "shot down"; military aircraft names
144750.explanation: The unit fires most strongly on the word "down" in "shot down" when the text is about a military pilot or aircrew being brought down in combat, usually in an air-force biography or a war film plot. A second, related group is the name of a military aircraft at the moment it is named (Vickers Wellington bomber, MQ-9 Reaper drone, SR-71 Blackbird). It reacts to the air-warfare meaning built up by the text before the token, not to the word "down" in general; a few weak, unrelated hits (code, a hospital list, a news report) do not fit. In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on the names of the hero's helpers (Nightwing, Robin, Batgirl, Gordon), which is at most loosely related through "wing" and the bird name.

144931.title: Completing an invented franchise name
144931.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the word piece that finishes (or nearly finishes) a distinctive proper name belonging to a film, TV or comic franchise, read inside a plot summary or episode article. Most are character surnames or unusual given names (Eobard, Swann, Halpert, Reyes, Altman, Bolin, Daggett, the 'ul' of Ra's al Ghul), with a second group of invented in-universe terms (Ba'ku, Ceti Alpha, CTU, Krabby Patties, Starling City, Second Impact). It fires at the point where the pieces add up to a recognisable fictional name, not on ordinary words or on common first names. Names of real or realistic places such as moons and towns (Phobos, Io, Triton, Hopewell) do not fire it; they belong to the opposite pole.

145519.title: Last piece of a specific proper name
145519.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a specific proper name, at the moment the name becomes recognisable from the words or word-pieces before it. Most of the strongest cases are named landmarks and sites (the Bloody Tower, Mount Herzl, Montjuïc, Hohenschwangau, Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, Heysel, hotel Sacher), with a second group of named people, characters and titles (Fritzl, Frau Cosima, Kirara, Li Yue, The Sky at Night, and in the plot summaries Rachel Dawes, then more weakly Bat-Signal, Wayne and Alfred); one code case (subjects_dir) fits only loosely. It is a reaction to the marked token as the closing piece of a name, often a foreign name split into several pieces, not to the meaning of the scene. Ordinary words, numbers, and generic location words such as 'station' or street numbers do not fire it.

145618.title: Control: steering a system or a person
145618.explanation: The unit fires on the word "control" (and close stand-ins such as "controlled from", "controllers", "directing", "calling the shots", "CTC", "driverless", "autoland") when the text is about one thing commanding or steering another. The strongest cases are technical: control theory and control engineering, distributed control systems, and railway or air traffic directed from a central control centre or signal box. In plot summaries it fires more weakly on the same idea applied to people: someone takes or assumes control of a person or machine, works them like a marionette, manipulates them, or is the mastermind, and on "control room". It reacts to the meaning of command and remote direction rather than to hands-on operating parts or ranks (pedals, clutch, quartermaster, executive officer), which belong to the opposite pole; one stray firing on a date ("August 7") does not fit.

147396.title: Word right after a clipped name or number
147396.explanation: The unit fires on the token that comes straight after a short, clipped or unusual name, code or number, at the moment that next token shows the name has ended and the sentence is moving on. In most of the strongest passages a longer form was seen earlier or would be expected (F11 then "F1 as", Vipera/Viperine then "Viper by", FAM46B then "FAM46 show", Roslagen then "Roslag Marine", Nandkumar then "Nand gets", US 62 then "US 6 via", Juror 11 and 12 then "Jurors 12 and 1 when", test_if_then_else then "test_if_then_stat"). The marked token itself varies (as, by, which, when, via, a verb, a dash or semicolon, the next part of a name), so the unit reacts to the boundary after the short form and not to a particular word. It does not fire after ordinary full-length words or names, and in the plot summaries it is only weak (after "Madame", "Non", "Keldysh", "Grand Budapest").

156371.title: The setting where a game or story happens
156371.explanation: The unit fires when the text names, or is about to name, the place in which the action of a game or story takes place: the "board", "arena", "world", "worlds", "levels" or "environment" of a game, and fictional cities and regions such as Liberty City, Gotham City or the Hoenn region. The peak sits either on the place word itself ("City", "world", "board", "house") or on the small word leading into it ("set in", "played on a", "explore an", "taking place in"). It is strongest in the gameplay sections of video-game and board-game articles and in opening sentences of plots ("In Gotham City, ..."). It is about a setting as the stage for play or story, not about places mentioned in passing, and not about the towed vessels, roots and trenches that the opposite pole shows.

159950.title: Small linking word early in opening sentence
159950.explanation: The unit fires within the first few words of the first running sentence of a document, or of the first real prose sentence after a heading, caption list or catalogue, on a small grammatical word that carries the sentence on (from, his, more, which, even, for, so, not, would, away, never, their, of, by, due, the Hindi 'to'). It is tied to position, not to any topic or particular word: in the plot summaries every firing is in the opening sentence. The same little words deep inside an ongoing text do not fire it, and content nouns and names rarely do. The pattern is loose, a position effect rather than a meaning.

163168.title: Role word tying a place to its owner
163168.explanation: Fires on the word that states what a named place or thing is in relation to a larger entity, just before that entity is named: above all "capital" in "Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia" or "the capital city Baku", and also "home to", "the official journal of", "publishes the Journal", "unidad de". It is strongest in the opening sentences of encyclopedia articles, where a city, building or organisation is being located by this kind of belonging. In plot summaries the weaker firings are on a possessor name inside a named property or institution ("Wayne" in Wayne Manor, Wayne Enterprises, Wayne Tower; "Pemberley, the grand Darcy estate"; "returns home to Gotham"). A plain generic noun for the thing itself ("house", "building", "issue", "cover") belongs to the opposite pole and does not fire.

171867.title: Dynasty names and sole rulers: tsar, rebbe, brothers
171867.explanation: The unit fires on a name or title that marks someone as the head or a member of a known line: a monarch or single supreme leader (tsar, monarchies, monarchical, King Uzziah, 'a supreme and permanent head', 'a living prophet'), the surname of a rabbinic dynasty (Soloveichik, Schneerson, Lubavitch, the Alter of Slabodka), or a family name or sibling being picked out from relatives already mentioned (Johann Bernoulli after Jacob, the Elric brothers, Luke beside Leia and 'another Skywalker', older brother Peter, Talia al Ghul, the horse Sistercharlie). It is reacting to what the text means, mid-name or on the title word, not to a particular spelling. In the plot summaries it also fires more weakly on the first mention of a famous titled figure (the Joker, Batman), and one strong passage (Art Ensemble of Chicago) does not fit, so the pattern is two related groups rather than one clean idea; ordinary names of unrelated people and ordinary politicians do not appear.

176751.title: Property word inside a set technical phrase
176751.explanation: No single clean idea. The unit fires on the word that names a defining property or state inside a fixed expression, usually just before the phrase is completed: chemistry terms ("double" bonds, Chinese 不飽和 "unsaturated" and 親和 "affinity", Palladium(II), "acidic" phospholipid, "hypercoag"ulable, half-"silvered" mirror), mind and perception terms ("conceptual" apraxia, abnormality of the "mind", ability to "think", criminally "insane", mental "condition", secret "identity", "clear" vision, see "through"), and a small group about being active at "night" / "noct"urnal. A few peaks (the code import "constraints", the product name XPI"LOT") fit none of these. It reacts to the token as the qualifier of a set term in expository text, not to any one word or topic, and ordinary uses of the same words outside such phrases are not shown firing.

177935.title: Code: start of a re-used member or argument
177935.explanation: Fires almost only in source code, on a token that joins access punctuation to the first piece of a name right after an object or function name: '.items', '.Def', '.Mail', '.refresh', '.dom', '(format', '(policy', '(value', '[ind', '/jquery'. In nearly every case the member, argument or path piece being started has already appeared earlier in the same file, so the unit marks the point where a known name starts to be used again. The few prose cases are the same thing in words and much weaker in plot summaries: the start of a name or phrase repeated from earlier (' V' in Verve Poetry Press, ' F' in a list of Farnsworths, 'AR 9 also' runs with, a repeated surname such as Falcone). Pieces in the middle of an identifier (camelCase or underscore suffixes) and names appearing for the first time do not fire it.

181098.title: Linking word opening a description of something
181098.explanation: Fires on the verb or small linking word that comes right after a thing has been named, at the point where the sentence starts to say what that thing is, is used for, is made of or consists of: "the collective is «used»", "Laboratory is «used»", "a Scarecrow «made» of garbage", "Damselfrau «consists» of", "the Shenk family--«which» consists of", "Jalisco isn't «what» he seems", "The killer is «dubbed»", "is not «a»", "was the «person»". It reacts to the grammatical slot (subject just named, its predicate or complement just opening), not to a topic; the peak words are mostly passive participles, relative "which", and prepositions such as of, in, for, on. Ordinary action verbs in narration, and the same words when they do not open such a description, are weak or silent; one source-code peak (context«['») does not fit, and the pattern is fairly loose.

181725.title: Connecting token right after a gap in text
181725.explanation: The unit reacts to position rather than meaning: it fires on a small connecting token (an opening bracket, a comma, a dash, "who", "a", "for", "one", "i.e.") that comes straight after a hole in the text, where a name, foreign term, date or link has been stripped out and left empty brackets or a double space ("The  (), who", "appeared in , a", "or  (isle of cloud)", "Le , la diffusion", "《》為"). It is most common in Wikipedia list entries, etymology notes and "See also"/reference sections, with a second, looser group in repetitive boilerplate code (indentation in a long run of Java GUI declarations, the ".html" ending a URL in a comment). The same function words in ordinary flowing prose fire only weakly (the plot-summary hits are all under 0.35), and a "that" or "the" introducing a clause after a named thing belongs to the opposite pole.

188341.title: Named substance or agent applied to something
188341.explanation: Fires on the name of a physical substance or agent at the moment it is brought in as the thing used on, mixed into or inflicted on something else: chemical reagents (sulfuric acid, quick-lime, alkaline carbonates, acetone), cooking ingredients being added (cornflour, flour, olive oil, turmeric), kinds of radiation (gamma rays, mind-control radiation), and in story plots the poison, drug or special material a character is hit with (fear toxin, hallucinogen, toxins, kryptonite-tipped, laced with). It often peaks partway through the substance word and usually follows wording like 'with', 'of', 'whisk in' or 'exposed to'. It does not fire on the same recipes or chemistry text at verbs, quantities or purposes, and a few weaker hits do not fit (keyword arguments in code such as connect_timeout and flags, the name Glinda, a magic mirror).

201972.title: Punctuation right after a missing number or phrase
201972.explanation: The unit fires on the comma, full stop or next word that arrives where a value should have been: text in which a measurement, figure, name or clause has been stripped out, leaving a gap such as "at depths between .", "temperatures ranging from .", "Output was ." or "which , and to fight". It reacts to what came before, a phrase that sets up an expected quantity or item (between, ranging from, a total of, according to legend), followed by nothing, and it does the same in Chinese (peaks on ， 。 並且). Ordinary punctuation after a complete phrase or a number that is actually present does not trigger it, which is why it is nearly silent in the well-formed plot summaries.

210540.title: Mixed: function values in code, things set up
210540.explanation: No single idea covers the strongest passages, and the peaks land on unrelated tokens ("for", a comma, "lambda", "function", "on", "through", a Korean syllable of "register"). The clearest group is source code where a function or wrapper object is being created on the spot and stored or passed as a value ("dtype = lambda", "config[name] = function", a cast to "Function<...>", "new ResultProxy", "startupArgs[0] = yield_"); plain "return function" and docstrings saying "Returns a function" belong to the opposite pole and do not fire it. The prose group is looser: something being arranged, assigned or prepared for a later purpose or term (a countdown "set for a year", jars filled with kerosene, nails and glass for a trap, yearly revenues "assigned", an appointment "to start on" a date, a socket that "can be used in", a vow of silence "until", bombs "planted"). The link between the two groups is weak, so treat this as a loosely understood unit.

220744.title: Inside a proposal for how things should be
220744.explanation: The unit fires inside the content of a proposal, suggestion or plan for something that does not exist yet: a TODO or FIXME note in code ("make configurable later", "both to config or external file", "Maybe log_backtrace: true"), a proposed name ("King Edward VII Street", "Maori Gratitude Day"), a suggested app feature ("Allow users to..."), a reform someone advocates ("the prisoner would...", "there ought to be laws", "suggested that all boats should", "replace the family name by a registered number"), a blueprint for a new section, or an imagined future invention ("you'll just press a knob"). It is reacting to the meaning of the preceding text, a frame of 'this is what should or could be done', not to the marked word, which varies widely. Plain description of how things already are or of what happened does not fire it; the weaker passages (a plot instruction, a sum of money) and the plot-summary sentences in section B fit only loosely.

230858.title: First piece of an expected topic name
230858.explanation: The unit fires on the opening or middle piece of a well-known compound name or fixed term whose rest is almost certain, when the text so far has already made that name the expected one: "Lois" (Lane) after Clark Kent and the Daily Planet, "Saddam" (Hussein), "Barack" (Obama), "Spider" (-Man), "Underground" (Railroad), "stained" (glass), "Dream" (time), "chick" (peas), "K-rypton-ian", "gu-ill-otined", "Chew" (bacca). In most cases the term is the subject of the document and has been used before, so the unit marks a familiar name being repeated or completed rather than any one meaning. It is weaker on names that are already whole in one token (Gotham) and does not respond to ordinary complete words or to names that arrive with no preparation in the context.

249243.title: Word that follows a just-named proper name
249243.explanation: The pattern is loose, but most of the strongest peaks fall on the word that comes straight after a proper name which opens a sentence, clause or heading, where that word says what belongs to or goes with the name: "Belden players", "Hieyas' soldiers", "Nissan drivers", "Ryker's drummer", "Bacon's arguments", "Van Loan's case", "Watt's assistance", "The Cherokee project", "Michigan assistant", "Hatton Promotions", "Lawrence, J.". A smaller group is the first verb after a title or name used as the subject ("1985 was released", "Rasputin Lives Mixed by", "Arkham Asylum is set", "Arkham Knight features"). A few peaks do not fit ("as he sketched", "become one", "and do not"), and in the plot summaries the unit is weak and lands on scattered function words ("him", "his", "for", "he"), so it is not a clean single idea; a name on its own, or an ordinary noun not attached to a name, does not appear to fire it.

256801.title: Start of a reported statement, belief or realisation
256801.explanation: The unit fires most often at the opening of a clause that gives the content of what someone says, thinks, knows or realises: on "that", or on the subject or first verb right after it ("realize that she is", "tells Mandrake that he believes", "experts say that", "told the server that it was", "Pat tells him that", "we knew right away that", "confesses to Murph that the crew was", "complain that"). It reacts to the situation set up by the preceding verb of telling, believing or realising, not to any particular marked word. About a third of the strong passages do not fit this (a comma before an explanation, "follows", "shapes", "desire", "yourself", a Chinese and a French token), so the pattern is real but loose; plain narration of actions without a reported claim or thought mostly does not fire it.

257645.title: Linking word before its complement (of, to, for)
257645.explanation: No single meaning: the unit fires on a short linking word, usually a preposition, that ties a noun or verb to something still to be named, as in "the screw of [the fan]", "the position of [the murderer]", "what do you think of [it]", "speaking to [Sonia's father]", "notably for [Enid Blyton]", "a transfer from [Chicago]", "a flight to [Dallas]". It reacts to the marked token in that mid-phrase position rather than to any topic, and the passages range across film plots, grammar articles, an etiquette book and code. A minority of peaks are other connectors or odd tokens ("is", "being", "including", "out", "treat", "found", an "=" inside a query string, a table bar "|", "add" in a Lisp example), so the pattern is loose. The same words also appear at the opposite pole in technical or code text ("values of type t"), so the word alone does not decide it.

262547.title: Second noun completing an "X and Y" pair
262547.explanation: The unit fires on the noun that completes a two-part noun phrase, almost always the word right after "and" (sometimes "or") in dry expository prose: "reports and services", "equipment and systems", "lava domes and flows", "gnostic literature and movements", "legislative aides and directors", "company or department". The second noun is typically a plain, general or plural noun that shares the modifier of the first one, and the unit reacts to that grammatical slot rather than to any particular word or topic (business boilerplate, navy ships, colleges and volcanoes all appear). A few cases are the second word of a compound without "and" ("pontoons tanks", "action figure", "destination time"). It does not fire on the "and" itself, on the first noun of the pair, or on "and" joining verbs or whole clauses.

276488.title: Joiner between two consecutive numbered items
276488.explanation: Fires on the connecting word or mark between two adjacent items of a numbered series, right after the first number and just before the second: "18th and 19th", "Games 2 and 3", "vols. 33 and 34", "figs. 6 and 7", "vol. I and II", "June 20 and 21", "January 18-19", "#3 & #4", German "Band I und Band II". The peak is on "and", "und", "&", a dash or the space after "and", so the unit seems to anticipate the next number in the pair or range (episodes, volumes, plates, issues, dates, rounds). It also fires on letter pairs like "P and Q", and only weakly on "and" joining two names ("Harry and Marv", "Mr and Mrs"); a lone number or an "and" joining ordinary phrases does not fire it.

306406.title: Mid-name in a famous story canon
306406.explanation: The unit fires part-way through a name, number or title that is a fixed piece of a very well-known story world, at the point where the text has made clear which canon is being discussed. It is strongest for the Chinese classic novels: the "108" Stars of Destiny / 108 bandits and "72" earthly fiends of Water Margin (Outlaws of the Marsh, Wu Song), and Journey to the West (Baigujing, Zhu Bajie, Monkey and his master), also in Chinese and Japanese text. More weakly it does the same inside names from other famous franchises and classics: Skywalker and "Star Wars", Arkham, Jor-El, Flashpoint, Hippolyta, Bennet. It reacts to the surrounding canon rather than to the marked token itself (the peaks are digits, word fragments and small words), and a few passages (a Python movie_list call, a release date) do not fit, so ordinary numbers or names outside such a recognised story world are not what drives it.

311592.title: Separator after a name in a list of people
311592.explanation: The unit fires on the comma, "and" or "or" that comes right after a named person when the text is joining or listing several people, so another name is about to follow ("Mitsuru, Yukari, Fuuka, and Aigis", "Elle and Emmett's wedding", "Gohan and Videl", "Benzema, Hazard, Luka Modric", "Claudius or Polonius"). It reacts to the position in the sentence, a name just finished and the next member of the group expected, not to any particular name; it is strongest in plot summaries and also appears in sports line-ups and cast lists. A few weaker firings do not fit ("with the help of", "doesn't", a closing question mark, a full stop after a score, a year), and commas or "and" that join clauses or things rather than named people are not what the strong examples show.

315315.title: Start of an invented name in fantasy lore
315315.explanation: The unit fires on the first piece (or an early piece) of a made-up proper name that belongs to a fictional universe: Tolkien's Ithilien, Vingilot and Dagor Dagorath, Nagini in Harry Potter, the Pokémon names Volcanion, Murkrow, Primeape, Kalos and Sea Crown, Hosnian Prime and Bendu in Star Wars, Lithone, Zhengyi, valar morghulis, Yubaba, Kohaku River, Clayface, House of El. It is strongest when the text before it is franchise lore (fantasy, science fiction, anime, games, comics) and has just set up a slot for a named thing, such as "a survivor of", "the Republic of", "revealed to actually be", "the shapeshifter"; it works in English, Spanish and Chinese alike. It reacts to the name beginning in that setting, not to one spelling. Ordinary real-world names, and the punctuation, dates and function words in the same kind of article, do not fire it.

316740.title: "Batman" in work titles; "Wheel-" names
316740.explanation: The unit reacts to particular word-pieces rather than to a meaning, and the passages fall into two unrelated groups. The first is the word "Batman" itself, most strongly when it is the opening word of a title or a name in a list of credits, voice roles, comic issues or cast ("The Batman", "Batman: Return of the Caped Crusaders", "Batman Forever", "Batman Villains Secret Files", "Batman (Kevin Conroy)"). The second is the piece "Wheel" at the start of a proper name (Wheeling in Ohio/West Virginia, Wheeler Oakman, Wheeler Winston Dixon, Wheelwright, and even the Chinese character for wheel in a word for rail ferry), with a couple of stray hits such as "coin" in bitcoinjs and "Bite" of Las Vegas. It does not fire on other superhero names or on other titles in the same lists, so it is tied to these spellings, not to superheroes or to lists in general.

327575.title: Japanese tokusatsu hero shows (Ultraman, Kamen Rider, Sentai)
327575.explanation: The unit fires when the surrounding text is about Japanese live-action transforming-hero franchises: Ultraman, Kamen Rider, Super Sentai, Metal Hero and Space Sheriff plots, cast lists and articles, in English or Chinese. The marked token varies widely (parts of hero names such as Dyna, Ultraman, Mebius, 霸王, but also commas, 'to', 'does', digits), so it is reacting to the topic already established, not to a particular word. At about half strength it also fires in Western superhero summaries where a hero's secret identity, alias or costume is mentioned ('reveals his identity', 'secret identity', 'adopting the alias'). Ordinary film plots, and years or sequel numbers in Western film franchises (the opposite pole), do not fire it.

335356.title: Substance carried in blood, water or air
335356.explanation: Fires when the text says a substance (a drug, toxin, virus, hormone, mineral, gas) is present in, enters, or is carried through a medium such as the blood, a body system, urine, a town's water supply, food or the air. The peak falls on the small linking word just before the medium is named ("in", "the", "through", "into", "'s", "her", "his", "entered", Spanish "en"), so it is anticipating a word like "blood", "water" or "atmosphere". Medical and physiology text gives the strongest cases, with contaminated-water and drugged-population plot lines close behind. The same linking words used for ordinary places or possession (a person in a room, someone's house) do not trigger it; it needs a chemical or agent already mentioned as the thing being located.

341047.title: Boundary where a new sentence or question starts
341047.explanation: The unit fires at the seam between a finished statement and the next one, in three related forms. One is the word "Can" opening a direct question right after a sentence ends ("Can you detect...", "can we observe...", "Can you please add...", "Can anyone estimate..."). The second is the full stop that closes a short setting-up sentence or a numbered clause heading just before the detail follows ("...relating to the Business.", "9. Breach of Contract.", "2.", "...is addicted.", and, more weakly, the period ending the opening scene-setting sentence of a plot summary). The third is an opening quotation mark right after "stated," or "read:" where a quoted statement is about to begin. It is not tied to any topic, and a few weaker peaks inside a phrase ("Make", "you", "-ing", "as") do not fit, so the idea is only moderately tight.

343225.title: Just before the expected object: "the money"
343225.explanation: Fires on the word that opens an object slot when the thing to be named is already obvious from the story, so it is anticipating the next word rather than reacting to the marked one. The main group is a verb of getting, keeping, handing over or carrying followed by a determiner, where the object is the loot or prize already established: "put the [money] in", "know where the [money] is", "retrieve the [gold]", "hired to retrieve the [money]", "refuses to hand [the winning ticket] over", "keep [the diamond and the money]", "swindled out of his [earnings]", "lose all [your money]"; the same slot also fires for non-money objects ("holds the [ball]", "lift the [object]", "the rest of the [posse]"). A weaker second group is the slot just before an exact figure is given ("serial number [23838]", "zone is [3996]", "receiving one [point]", "150.[75]"). It does not fire on the word "money" itself or on an ordinary "the" after a preposition introducing a place or owner ("at the funeral home", "owner of the club"), which is the opposite pole.

356911.title: Midway through a famous fictional franchise name
356911.explanation: The unit fires partway through a well-known multi-word name from superhero, fantasy or science-fiction franchises, on the token just before the name's distinctive ending: "League of" (Assassins / Shadows), "Hand of" (the King), "Knights of" (the Old Republic), "Order of the" (Phoenix), "Two-F" (ace), "Ph" (antasm / antom Zone / antosaur), "the Blue" (Beetle), "Gold" (Zeo Ranger), "the" (Super Saiyans). It is reacting to what comes next: the text so far has set up a named group, office, villain or place of a fictional universe and the rest of the name is predictable. It works across languages (Spanish "Mano del Rey", Chinese Palpatine) and in plots, lists and news alike. Ordinary uses of "of", "the" or a colour word that are not inside such a franchise name do not fire it; a few weaker cases ("chosen by the producers", "last surviving Namekian") are only loosely related.

361617.title: Perfect auxiliary after a third-person subject
361617.explanation: The unit fires on the helping verb of a perfect tense ("has", "have", "had", French "a" in "a été", sometimes "was", "been" or the "now" in "had now") right after a noun-phrase subject, usually a thing rather than a person, in a plain statement that reports a state brought about by something that already happened: "the ring has been returned", "lit torches have been placed", "the token seems to have expired", "until new data has arrived". It is strongest when a past participle, often "been" plus a passive verb, is about to follow, and it works the same in film plots, encyclopedia prose and code comments or error messages. It does not fire on "have" in questions addressed to someone ("Where have you been?", "have you ever"), which belong to the opposite pole, nor on "has" meaning possession except weakly.

363491.title: Linking word just before a villain's name
363491.explanation: This unit fires on the small linking token that comes immediately before a fictional villain or antagonist is about to be named: "at the hands of" Lord Voldemort, "captured by" the Nome King, "run by" the evil Dr. Noah, "working for" Buddy Pine or Harvey Dent, "resistance to" Voldemort, "old nemesis," the Sheriff of Nottingham, "arch-villain" Blofeld, "criminal mastermind" Lex Luthor, "villains in Gotham City:" the Joker. It is predictive: the peak is on the preposition, comma, colon or verb (by, of, for, to, from, as, with, kills, stop), not on the villain's name, and the text before it has set up an enemy, threat or evil force. A weaker related group is the cast-list slot before a character's name ("Jonathan Pryce as" the Master, "Judi Dench as", "Kevin Conroy voices"). The same prepositions and commas before heroes, team members or ordinary people do not fire it; lists of protagonists belong to the opposite pole.

366061.title: Word-piece "conv" starting an unfinished word
366061.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the fragment "conv" (or Spanish "con-ve") when it is the first piece of a longer, rarer word that still has to be completed, such as convulse/convulsing/convulsions, convalesce/convalescing, convoluted, convolution/convolve, convective/convected and Convict. The meaning of the surrounding text does not matter: it fires alike in film plots, physics, mathematics, source code and Spanish. It is much weaker on the longer piece "convin" of "convinces" (about 0.3 to 0.4), and nothing shows it firing on common conv- words that are a single token; the opposite pole takes the similar-sounding "Kon" of Konstantin and Konrad.

372199.title: Inside WWII aircraft, U-boat and unit designations
372199.explanation: The unit fires in encyclopedic military history of the Second World War, at a point inside the name or designation of a piece of hardware or a unit: the space or hyphen between a maker's abbreviation and its number (Junkers Ju 88, Ju 87, U-13), the abbreviation of a German air wing (JG 27, Staffel, Kampfgeschwader 26/51), the 'U' of U-boat / U-Boote, 'flying' of flying boat, and 'Sur' of the Battle of Surigao Strait; the same happens in Chinese articles on Japanese carrier bombers. It reacts to the surrounding situation (air and naval warfare, mostly German Luftwaffe and submarine terms) more than to one word, and it peaks mid-name, just before the designation is completed. Ordinary story text hardly fires it: in plot summaries it gives only weak echoes on look-alike fragments (Suriname, war-surplus submarine, German U-boat, Flying Graysons, Ra's al Ghul), and general mentions of war or planes without a type or unit designation do not fire it.

372323.title: Linking word before a DC Comics place-name
372323.explanation: The unit fires in Batman, Superman and other DC Comics stories on a small linking word, usually a preposition of place ("at", "to", "in", "into", "from", "on", "of", "called", or the end of "infiltrate"), at the moment when a well-known fixed name from that universe is about to follow: Wayne Manor, Arkham Asylum, the Batcave, LexCorp, Metropolis, Smallville, the Daily Planet, the Fortress of Solitude, Themyscira, or a stock character such as Bruce Wayne or Lois Lane. It is anticipating the next word, not reacting to the preposition itself: the same "at" or "to" in an ordinary film plot, or in a superhero text where no canonical location or name is due, does not fire. A few weaker cases are the same anticipation in lists and credits (a set number, "Battle for the Cowl", "member of the original team").

373146.title: Slot where a familiar character's name comes
373146.explanation: Fires in text about films, TV series, anime and comics at the point where a specific, well-known person is about to be named or has just started to be named. In the reference corpus the peak is on the role, relation or linking word directly before the name: 'pirate captain' before Monkey D. Luffy, 'Captain' before Jack Sparrow, 'his father' before Thomas, 'his wife' before Iris, 'starring' before Mayumi Tanaka, 'KJ Apa as' before Archie Andrews, 'Edward Kitsis and' before Adam Horowitz; in the plot summaries it sits on the first piece of the name itself (Max, Thomas, Catherine, the Z of Zod). So it reacts to what comes next, a predictable character, actor or writer name from a familiar franchise (One Piece, Pirates of the Caribbean, The Flash, Lost, Hannah Montana), not to the marked word. The same kind of linking word before a company or event name ('by Kenner', 'at Comic-Con') does not fire it, and one strong passage (the '2' of a 2013 air date) does not fit the pattern.

374913.title: Plant-derived foods, seeds, oils and extracts
374913.explanation: Fires in text about food crops and the products made from plants: seeds, oilseeds, grains, cereals, nuts, flour, bran, soy, essential oils and vitamins, in English, Russian, Korean and Chinese alike. The peak usually lands inside or just before the name of such a product or in the middle of a list of them ("fruits, grains", "fiber and seed", "soy lecithin", "essential oils", "cereal and oilseed", "ground into flour"), and also on food-policy names such as the World Food Prize or a Food Security Act. In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on the first word of a named substance or its plant source ("fear toxin", "fear gas", "Joker venom", "kryptonite", "blue flowers" that yield a compound). Pure biochemistry naming and ingredient lists of chemicals belong to the opposite pole, so chemical vocabulary alone is not enough; the strongest firings need the crop or food-product setting.

376466.title: Linking word before a fictional world's named place or clan
376466.explanation: Fires in summaries of serial fiction (soap operas such as Neighbours, Dynasty, Emmerdale and Coronation Street, and the Transformers franchise) on the small linking word that comes just before the story's own named setting, family or faction: "returns to" Erinsborough, "arriving in" Ramsay Street, "arrived at" The Woolpack, "revolves around the" Carringtons, "patriarch of" the Buchanan family, "war between the" Autobots and Decepticons. It reacts to what is about to come next (the proper name of the fictional place or group the character belongs to or arrives at), not to the preposition itself; in the plot summaries it does the same before Gotham City, the crime scene, Isla Nublar and Gotham Zoo. Prepositions before ordinary real-world places or objects, and lists of titles of series or comics, do not fire it.

376737.title: First name "John" after an official's title
376737.explanation: Fires on the first name "John" at the moment it opens the full name of a man who has just been introduced by an office or job title, above all American government lawyers and security officials: "White House counsel John Dean", "former Attorney General John N. Mitchell", "his boss, John Ashcroft", "FBI Special Agent John Connolly", "under John Doar". It is strongest in Watergate, Justice Department, FBI and national-security writing; in the plot summaries it fires more weakly on other J first names after a role (Jonathan Crane, Jack Ryder, Jack Napier, John Daggett, John Blake, Jefferson Skeevers, James "Jim" Gordon). A small separate group is a digit in the middle of a year ("19«1»7", "20«1»4", "18«9»1"). It does not fire on "John" as a middle name or on a John with no official role ("Daniel John Cannon", bar manager "John A. Kelly", "Justice John Marshall Harlan" got no peak), nor on the title words themselves.

379403.title: Family name naming a house, firm or shop
379403.explanation: The unit fires on a surname at the moment it is being used as the name of a place or business that belongs to that person or family, just before the noun that says what kind of place it is: Wayne Manor, Wayne Enterprises, Wayne Medical, the Suzuki Loom Manufacturing Co., Saotome Research Lab, the Li family estate, Tachibana's, Kilmer House, and Japanese or Chinese family shops and breweries (Arai kimono shop, Nakagami brewery, Yamaoka engine workshop, Po-chi-lam clinic). The family or founder has usually been named earlier, and the sentence is typically sending someone to that location ('visits', 'returns to', 'at', 'under'). It does not fire on the same surname when it simply names a person (Bruce Wayne, Thomas Wayne, Michio Suzuki).

382272.title: Rank or job title before a character's name
382272.explanation: Fires on a rank or job word used as a label directly in front of a character's personal name in a story summary, at the moment the name is about to follow: "Valkyrie pilot" Hikaru Ichijyo, "intelligence officer" Cassian Andor, "Security Chief" Worf, "Second Officer" Data, "ensign" Lalah Sune, "Dr. Leonard" McCoy, "Lt." Uhura. It is strongest for military and starship crew in science fiction (Star Trek, Gundam, Macross, Space: 1999, Star Wars), and in the Batman summaries it fires on police ranks before Gordon's name ("Lieutenant", "Detective", "Commissioner", "Sergeant") and on "police officer" or "ally" before a name. A rank or job word that is not introducing a named character, and class labels before scientific names ("the bacterium", "species of"), do not fire.

383205.title: Just before an honorific title is bestowed
383205.explanation: Fires on the small linking word (the, of, a, as) that follows a verb of recognition and comes right before an honorific designation of a person: 'recognize as one of the Righteous Among the Nations', 'the title of Servant of God / Venerable', 'also known as the Baba Sali', 'taught by the Baal Shem Tov', and in Russian 'numbered among the saints' and 'the title of Hero'. It reacts to what is about to come rather than to the marked word: the text has set up that someone is being formally named, beatified, canonized or revered, and the title is expected next. In the plot summaries the same pattern is weaker and secular: a character is publicly hailed, honored or mourned 'as a hero', becomes 'a public hero', or is declared 'a wanted criminal'. A few peaks fall on year digits or other tokens inside articles about Holocaust rescuers, rabbis and saints and do not fit this exactly; ordinary 'as a' or 'the' before a job or plain description (such as 'working as a minister' earlier in the same articles) is not among the peaks.

384684.title: About to name a just-introduced person or substance
384684.explanation: The unit fires at the moment a specific name is about to be supplied or has only just begun, right after the text has set up who or what is coming by a role or relation: "a woman named" [Helen], "spy Phillip" [Vandamm], "his valet, P"[assepartout], "investigator Philip", "Lieutenant" [Joshi], "his butler," [Alfred], "gun dealer" [Easy Andy], "their accountant," [Lau]. So it reacts to what comes next, not to the marked token: the peak sits on a comma, a title (Mr., Lieutenant), the word "named", or the first letter of the name (often P). A smaller related group is a specific chemical or item about to be named ("biosynthesis of" [morphine], "toxins, particularly", "isola a" [Morfina]) and the middle of a year in a film list ("The Dark Knight (20"). It does not fire on names that are already established and simply repeated, or on role words that are not followed by a new name.

385661.title: "Designed by" before an architect or firm
385661.explanation: The unit fires on the word "by" in "designed by" (also "design by", "undertaken by") in articles about buildings, at the point where the name of the architect, architecture firm or builder is about to come: Bates Smart, Levitt Goodman, Fender Katsalidis, Daryl Jackson, Roy Grounds. It is anticipating a design or construction firm's name rather than reacting to the word "by" itself; weaker firings come just before other named firms, venues, publishers or architects ("Balmond at" Arup, "Vienna:" Edition Selene, "William" Kent, "Wiener" Musikverein). Ordinary uses of "by" (killed by, voiced by) and the commas before character names in plot summaries give only faint activity, so in story text it is nearly silent.

385893.title: Linking word before a wrestling or franchise name
385893.explanation: The unit fires on a small connecting word or punctuation mark (by, of, as, on, with, in, then, a comma or colon) at the point where the next words are almost certainly the proper name of an entertainment company or franchise title. The strongest cases are professional-wrestling articles just before "World Wrestling Federation", "World Championship Wrestling", WWF or WCW ("produced by", "hired by", "signed a contract with", "then known as"), with a second group just before Marvel or Batman titles ("Marvel vs. Capcom:", "Marvel Anime:", "Catwoman in" Batman Returns). It is reacting to what is about to come, not to the marked word itself: the same words by, of, in or with in ordinary prose, where no well-known promotion, studio or franchise name is due next, do not fire it. The plot-summary sentences are weaker and looser (before "DC Animated Universe", "General Zod", "Gotham City", a list of villains).

388994.title: Before a linked person's name; 'to' mid-word
388994.explanation: Two groups. The main one is the slot just before the given name of a person who is tied to someone already mentioned: a kin or role word, or the comma, "and" or bracket that follows it (her« husband» Julius, her« son» Ryszard, his son« John», a neighbor«,» Hannah, his butler«,» Alfred Pennyworth, Ethel« and» Julius Rosenberg, Thomas «and» Martha, the« character» Sally Bowles, Stalin («born» Ioseb), so the unit seems to anticipate the coming name of a spouse, relative, servant, partner or alias. The second group is only a spelling: the "to" / "sto" piece in the middle of a word, as in H«isto»ire, hist«o»ires, esc«rito»ire, sa«uto»ir, «to»isons and Japanese ヒ«スト»リー. A comma or "and" that is not about to introduce a named partner or relative does not appear to fire it.

391802.title: Satellite and spacecraft names; Robin/Titans heroes
391802.explanation: The strongest passages fall into two groups rather than one clean idea. The larger group is text about satellites, spacecraft, missiles and military craft, where the unit fires as a named system or designation begins or is about to be given (IN-MARSAT, IN-TELSAT, 'launch of' Astra 1K, 'USS' Vincennes, Pol-aris missile, SH-2G Seasprite, 'NORAD ID:', Laser Altimeter '(' MOLA, Ka band 'inter'-satellite links, the Russian 'spacecraft', shooting 'down' a spy satellite). The second group is DC young-hero text around Robin, Nightwing and the Teen Titans (Rav-ager, 'Robin I /' Dick Grayson, 'Nightwing (' Dick Grayson) together with bat-named vehicles and gear (Batcopter, Batmobile, bat-ladder). It reacts to the surrounding subject, not to the marked token, which varies widely (slashes, brackets, prepositions, name fragments), so a name or acronym outside these two subjects is not what it responds to.

392617.title: Last word before a sentence or clause ends
392617.explanation: Fires on the final word of a phrase that is now complete, just before a full stop, comma or joining word, so it reacts to what comes next (a stop) more than to the marked word itself. The strongest cases are mathematics articles in English, German and Portuguese where a formula symbol has been stripped out, leaving a small word such as "in", "of", "for", "and", "de" or "von" standing directly before the full stop ("a subset of exactly one set in ."). The weaker cases are ordinary sentence endings: "the 197th episode overall.", "longer than that.", "km².", "in Österreich.", "Mary Jane Watson.", "North Dakota.", "witnessed the scene." The same words in the middle of a phrase that clearly continues do not trigger it, and the marked words share no meaning, so the pattern is one of position rather than topic.

393632.title: Linking word just before a named party
393632.explanation: The unit fires on a connecting word at the point where the text is about to name a specific other party: "joined" before the club a footballer moves to, "for" before a record label or tour, "with" or "and" before a companion or co-performer, a comma or opening bracket before the next name in a list, and relation words such as "daughter", "niece" or "protégé" before the person's name. It reacts to what is coming next (a proper name of a club, company, person or species) rather than to the marked word itself, and is strongest in biography-style sentences about footballers and musicians. A few strong passages do not fit (the middle of a Russian word, "right-angles to", "in 1527,"), so the pattern is loose; the same words in ordinary phrases with no name about to follow are not among its strongest firings.

394314.title: Lead-in to a named school, team or person
394314.explanation: Fires at the point where a specific proper name is about to be given or has just begun, usually on the small word before it (the, of, from, form, a comma) or on the role word or first name that leads into it. The largest group is universities, colleges and their sports teams (the Golden Hurricane, the University of Tulsa, the University of Oslo, Fordham, the Wake Forest Demon Deacons, the Merage and Marriott business schools); a second group is a person named right after a relationship or job (his sister, Mia Toretto; former friend Eduardo Saverin; head coach Todd Graham), and in the plot summaries it is almost always the first name Barbara just before Gordon or Wilson. It looks like anticipation of the name that comes next more than a reaction to the marked word itself. It is not every such lead-in: very similar phrases such as 'a degree at the University of ...' fire the opposite pole instead, and the passages do not show what separates the two.

395560.title: First piece of a distinctive name being introduced
395560.explanation: The unit fires on the opening fragment of a specific, unusual proper name or identifier whose remainder is still to come, usually right after a phrase that sets up a name: 'the shapeshifter Clay-(face)', 'the villain H-(ush)', 'henchman H-(ackett)', 'in X-(ibalba)', 'confronts X-('tabay)', 'escape from Al-(catraz)', 'named Brother (Eye)', 'near Fort (Tiuna)', 'along with L-(obo)'. In source code the same thing happens at the start of a library or class identifier (d3, X9ObjectIdentifiers, grunt.log). It is about the start of the name, not the subject matter; it does not fire on ordinary words, on later pieces of a name, or on common names that need no completing. The examples are fairly mixed (comic villains, Maya underworld names, code), so the reading is only moderately firm.

397742.title: Capital H beginning a name, rest still to come
397742.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a lone capital "H" that the tokenizer has split off as the first letter of a longer word, almost always a proper name or foreign term whose remainder has not been read yet (Rhenish H-esse, H-unsrück, H-engst, H-apuonone, H-ine-nui-te-pō, H-urrat, H-undtstößer, H-irundo, H-ume's owl, H-awke's Bay, the H-ab, Jabba the H-utt, H-ush, Mad H-atter). It fires more weakly on other single capital letters in the same position or named as letters (T, M, D in "DTP", R in "Riddler", Russian "д"). A lower-case "h" starting a word, as in old-spelling "hys", "hir", "hauing" or "hôtel", does not fire it and belongs to the opposite pole, and the meaning of the surrounding text (geography, mythology, birds, villains) does not matter.

398548.title: Mid-compound characters of titles in Chinese articles
398548.explanation: Fires almost only deep inside long Chinese encyclopedia articles (mostly Traditional script, Taiwan-related), on one character in the middle of a compound, most often the name of a post or an institution: 總«裁» (president), 理事«長» / 州«长» / 校«長» (chairman, governor, principal), 聯«邦»調查局 (federal bureau), «海»軍 (navy), «前»僱員 (former employee), or a district name such as «大»安區 and 松«山». English text fires much more weakly but in the same shape, on a word inside an office or organisation title (State Board« of» Education, board «member», «Police» Commissioner, May«or»). Several peaks are ordinary words (資料, 個, 被, 柔和, a digit), so the title-or-office reading covers only part of it; the firmest common factor is the Chinese article setting, and ordinary English prose with no title being spelled out stays low.

398907.title: About to say "a different/unique/specific" something
398907.explanation: The unit fires on a linking verb or preposition (has, have, to, with, taking, containing, make, induce) at the point where the next words are expected to say that each member of a group has its own distinct property: "each has ... a unique set", "each taking ... a different position", "each dedicated to ... a particular theme", "layers with ... differing characteristics", "more than one genetically ... distinct". It is driven by what comes next, not by the marked word: the subject is usually "each", "different X" or a plural set, and the unit anticipates an adjective such as different, distinct, unique, specific, particular or own. The same verbs and prepositions in ordinary narration do not fire it strongly; in the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on "the", "of" or "his" before a specific named thing.

400670.title: Linking token just before a predictable name
400670.explanation: The unit fires on a small linking token at the point where the context makes one specific name or term about to follow, rather than on the name itself. Three groups stand out: Batman and Gotham franchise text ("Batman:" before "The Animated Series" or "The Brave and the Bold", "district attorney" before Harvey Dent, "played by" before the actors, "related to" before the Batman franchise, "researcher at" before Wayne Enterprises); NASCAR and motor-racing text, where it fires on the first name "Dave" before a driver's or announcer's surname (Blaney, Steele, Moody, Burns, Davey Allison); and blood-clotting test text (an opening bracket after a test name, "perform a" before "mixing test"). The same words (by, to, at, a, a colon, Dave) in text where nothing particular is expected next do not appear, and the groups share only this about-to-name position, so it is not one clean topic.
