402677.title: Role description just before a character's name
402677.explanation: The unit fires at the point where a describing phrase has just finished and the specific name of a person or character is about to be given: "mobster [Sal Maroni]", "arch-foe [the Cheetah]", "archenemy, [Professor Eobard Thawne]", "crime boss [Carmine Falcone]", "antiquities dealer [Diana Prince]", "holy warrior [Azrael]", "old acquaintance [Lady Shiva]", "the last Lodi sultan, [Ibrahim Lodi]". The marked token is the last word of the role (boss, dealer, warrior, mobster, foe) or a small linking token that introduces the name (a comma, "as", "called", "a.k.a.", "with", "and", "of", "by"), and sometimes the first piece of the name itself ("Bar" of Barneys, "Var" of Varadarāja). It is strongest in comic-book and superhero texts where a villain, ally or relative is being introduced by name, but also appears in history and fashion articles; it does not fire on role words used on their own with no name to follow, and plain kinship phrases such as "wife of" or "son of" before a famous name belong to the opposite pole.

403759.title: Naming police bodies, ranks and custody places
403759.explanation: Fires in factual, encyclopedia-style text about police and criminal-justice institutions, at the small linking token that sits inside or just after an official title or agency name and leads into the proper name: "99th precinct of the [New York Police Department]", "Office for Police Conduct (", "Commissioner, [Metropolitan Police]", "police commissioner [James Gordon]", "Chief of [Police]", "detainees at [Guantanamo]", "interrogate Joker at [Arkham Asylum]". The peak token itself is usually a function word, bracket or first name (the, of, at, on, "(", James), and in biographies of police chiefs and articles on police court cases it also lands on year digits and on legal-status phrases such as "released on bail" and "put on trial". It is the institutional, name-and-title side of law enforcement; the action side (arrest warrants, marshals and bounty hunters bringing someone in, a police dragnet) belongs to the opposite pole and does not fire it.

405930.title: Word-initial letter V, strongest in Balkan-Ottoman text
405930.explanation: The unit fires on a lone "V" or "v" token that begins a word whose remaining letters come next: «V»ardar, «V»lachs, «V»ize, «V»lora, «V»assiliada, «v»assals, «V»engeance, «v»engeful, «v»illage, «v»iento, «v»ial, «v»owing and the split "super«v»illains". It is strongest when the surrounding text is about the Balkans, Greece, Macedonia and the Ottoman Turks, and in that setting it also fires on a few non-V tokens just before or after the word for Turks in Greek and Russian (του«ς» Τούρκους, турок« в», the quote mark before εκτουρκισμός). Outside that setting the same letter fragment still fires, but only at about half strength. Words beginning with v that are written as one whole token, and Balkan or Ottoman passages with no v-initial word at the peak, are not what it picks out.

406598.title: Midway through a multi-word term or name
406598.explanation: Fires on a non-final word or word-piece inside a fixed multi-word term or name, at the point where the rest is predictable: anatomical and histological terms (flexor car-pi radialis, ligament-um longitudinale, Huerthle cell carcinoma, Leydig cells, sebaceous gland, parenchymes de reserve, four main bearings) and institution or title names (Detroit Museum of Art, Buffalo Central High School, St. John's University, Green Lantern Corps, District Attorney Harvey Dent, Gotham City Police Department, police Commissioner James Gordon, Dick Grayson). It reacts to the position (a modifier or first part with the head noun or surname still to come), in any language, not to a particular word. It does not fire on the last word of such a term, nor on the same words used alone in ordinary prose; the opposite pole takes the plain 'the' before a sports team name.

413586.title: Just before naming a notorious actor or target
413586.explanation: The unit fires on the small linking word or role label that comes immediately before a controversial party is named or described, so it is reacting to what is about to come next rather than to the marked word. In the reference corpus this is news-style writing about political violence, extremism and scandal: 'the incident at' (the Capitol), 'his personal lawyer' (Michael Cohen), 'now-banned' (Muslim Brotherhood), 'controlled by the' (militants of Hamas), 'leader of' (Svoboda), 'rammed a' (car into a crowd), 'the ousting of' (Morsi), 'criminal probe of' (the Trump Organization). In the plot summaries the same slot is the job label before a criminal or powerful figure's name: 'crime boss', 'mob boss', 'mobster', 'industrialist', 'their accountant,'. It is weaker and looser in plots, and it does not fire on the name itself; the closely similar slot before a named terrorist attack or bombing site ('blamed Pakistan for the attack', 'over Lockerbie') belongs to the opposite pole.

413688.title: Partway through a specific name, title or quote
413688.explanation: The unit fires on an early or middle piece of a fixed string that still has to be completed from memory, not on any one word. Three related groups appear: a given name just before its surname in a credit or list of people (Frank Caviggia, George Kurtz, Mark Topham, Scott Banister, Joe Quesada, Ignacio), a small linking word inside a song or film title or a quoted line ("It's Alright", "The Joker Is Wild", "Jesus Is Just Alright", "Des is a Wahnsinn", "You Are My Lucky Star", "It's Chinatown", Duncker &, United States Geological Survey), and the first word of a two-word character name (Red Hood, Green Goblin, Mad Hatter). Several of the very strongest cases are in the middle of Latvian words or a Latvian saying and one Japanese place name, so foreign-language text being reproduced verbatim is a strong trigger too. It does not fire on the last word of a name or title, or on the same words (is, just, red, mad) in ordinary prose; the pattern is loose and the opposite pole also lands on first pieces of names.

414287.title: Contested topic named before denier/skeptic label
414287.explanation: Fires in text about denialism, conspiracy theories, anti-vaccine or anti-science movements and the people who fight or spread them, usually on the word naming the disputed subject (Holocaust, AIDS, global warming, 9/11, COVID-19, Sinovac, Nazi, animal) right before a label such as denier, denialism, skeptics, truther, misinformation, cultists, experts or thieves. It reacts to the meaning of the preceding text and anticipates the scornful or partisan label, so it also fires on nearby tokens (a year, 'countering', 'of') inside articles about skeptics and critics of alternative medicine. Neutral mentions of the same topics outside a controversy or name-calling frame do not fire it; the plot-summary hits are weak and only loosely related (labels like sidekick, serial killer, Joker venom).

416525.title: Noun about to take "-laden" or "-laced"
416525.explanation: The unit fires on the first half of a hyphenated compound that means "full of, loaded with or marked by X": on the noun itself or on the "-l" that begins the ending, as in profanity-laced, innuendo-laden, expletive-laden, explosives-laden, moisture-laden, silt-laden, fish-laden, bullion-laden, feedback-laden, kryptonite-laced, venom-laden. It is anticipating the ending, so it fires just before "laden" or "laced" is completed. Related compounds fire more weakly (effects-heavy, TLP-labeled, crime-ridden, guilt-ridden, booby-trapped, neon-tinged). The same nouns used on their own, without a following "-laden"-type ending, and other hyphenated compounds such as "ball-winning" or "even-tempered" do not fire it.

422114.title: First piece of a trade or office word
422114.explanation: The unit fires on the opening fragment of a longer word that the model has split into pieces, mostly in French and German text: "bour", "Bou", "bra" (bourreaux, boulangère, bourgmestre, braconnier) and above all "Ver"/"ver" (Verlag, Verleih, Verwaltungskaufmann, Reiseveranstalter, verpachtet, Verbindungen). In the strongest cases the word being started names what someone is or does for a living or in office (executioner, baker, mayor, poacher, clerk, judge, publisher, distributor, tour operator), so the unit seems to react to the start of a trade, office or business noun rather than to the spelling alone; a few "Ver-" hits are not occupations. In the English plot summaries it fires only weakly, on a rank or first name that starts naming a person right after a job description ("Captain" Ellen Yindel, police "officer" John Blake, second-in-command "Jack" Napier, predecessor "James" Gordon). Ordinary complete English words, and the middle or end of such words, do not fire it.

428032.title: First fragment of a word already guessable
428032.explanation: The unit fires on the first piece of a word or name that is split into pieces, at a point where the earlier text already makes clear how it will finish. Most often the piece is a lone s or S (sheet pan S-ausage, pygments_style = 's-phinx', ranger and s-apper tabs, student-s-oldier, s-weat box, Anarcho-S-yndicalist, S-estak, S-ons of the Batman, Bat-s-ignal); the other recurring cases are Ind- of Indiegogo after crowdfunding or fundraising talk, Ark- of Arkham before Asylum or State Hospital, kos in Ceskoslovensk-, and KO- of the station call sign KOVR. Weaker firings fall on 'a' just before an expected noun (through a window, down a well). Whole ordinary words beginning with s, and word starts whose continuation is not predictable from context, do not fire it.

428929.title: Second-to-last piece of a long transliterated name
428929.explanation: The unit fires in the middle of a multi-piece word, on the piece just before a final piece that is all but certain, so it is reacting to what comes next. The strongest cases are foreign place names spelled out sound by sound in Chinese, Japanese, Korean or Hindi, caught on the syllable before the closing '-a': 尼 in 羅馬尼亞, 愛沙尼亞, 加泰羅尼亞, 塔斯馬尼亞, 維 in 塞爾維亞 and 斯堪的納維亞, 西 in 馬來西亞, 里 in 利比里亚, 니 in 펜실베이니아, ड in फ़्लोरिडा, and ネ in チャンネル. A few are other half-finished words (a.F.r.I.c before A, UR before ITemplate, Hindi सुंदरता and मल्टीमीडिया). It does not fire on whole words or on the first piece of a name, and in English plot text it is weak (under half strength), landing on mid-word fragments such as 'Sedgew', 'Pyromani', 'All-Americ' or the 'W' of 'Wicked' and 'Winkies'.

440010.title: Just before an upcoming "as" / "-ase" syllable
440010.explanation: This unit reacts to what is about to come next, not to the marked token: it fires on the word piece right before a syllable spelled or sounding like "as" - "ascent", "_ascii", "Aspen", "asiatica", "Asiama", the final "-as" of Caiaphas, poison-gas and GraphBLAS, Russian "п|аспорта" and "авиаб|аза", and "Ark|ham", where "Asylum" is the expected next word. Its strongest hits are a related group in Korean: the first syllable of the loanwords base, baseball and suitcase (베|이스, 케|이스), with looser cases on 벤(치마크) and Chinese 基(特峰), a character that itself means "base". The marked tokens share nothing with each other (a quote mark, "new", "Johnson", "geo", "ham", "et"), and the unit does not fire on the "as" itself or on these words when no "as" syllable is due next. Text standing before a double-s "ass" (passen, canvassed, Haas) looks similar but does not fire this pole.

446669.title: Fixed set of unrelated rare tokens
446669.explanation: This first-layer unit reacts to the marked token itself, and there is no single meaning behind it: it fires on a fixed handful of unrelated tokens whatever the context. The recurring ones are the Arabic ' بصورة' ('in a ... manner'), the Korean syllable '끼' (as in 새끼), the Java identifier piece 'AlgorithmException', the Chinese '热血传奇', '被淘汰' and '舂', the Japanese 'というもの', odd single letters (Greek 'Ἔ', Thaana 'ވ', insular 'ꝺ'), and, at about half strength, the word 'Gotham' in plot summaries. Most are long or rare single tokens in non-Latin scripts, but other text in the same languages and the surrounding words do not fire it.

451471.title: Token right after a number ending in 1
451471.explanation: The unit fires on the token that comes immediately after a number whose last digit is 1 (2001, 2011, 215001, 113001, 63001, 11, 51, or a lone 1), when that token is not another digit: a range dash ("2001-2007", "215001–215100", "#1-4"), "of" ("Image 1 of 1", "Part 1 of the book"), "years" ("11 years", "51 years"), or the Chinese and Japanese year character 年 ("2001年", "2011年底"). It is a surface, token-level reaction to the preceding digit 1, not to meaning, and it works the same in English, Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese and source code. Weaker firings come on word-pieces after a lower-case letter l, which looks like a 1 ("l-ured", "l-ingers"), and faintly on a digit after 1 ("$18,000"); the same words after numbers ending in other digits fire little ("10 years" is weak), and a 0 following 1 belongs to the opposite pole.

454387.title: Bracket or equals sign right after a number
454387.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: an opening bracket or an equals sign that comes directly after a number, as in the statute and tax-code labels "section 10(b)" and "501(c)(3)", model numbers like "20380(20385)" and "300(S)", and sums or equations like "843 ÷ 20 =" and "log 10=". It is strongest when the bracket is glued to the digits and opens a short letter or number label; in the plot summaries it fires more weakly on a bracket that opens after a year or an issue number ("1955 (", "#489-490 (") and faintly on other small words right after a number ("1940 at", "$40,000 in"). Brackets or equals signs that follow ordinary words, and the tilde between two numbers in a range (the opposite pole), do not trigger it.

460110.title: The names Superman and Batman, at the token
460110.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the piece 'man' that completes 'Superman', and the single token 'Batman'. It is a spelling-level response, not a meaning-level one: it also fires on 'man' in lower-case 'batman' (an officer's servant), in 'Supermanica', on a nickname 'Superman' for a construction worker or an object, and on the Chinese character 人 that completes 超人 (Superman). It is strongest when the name opens a sentence, a title or a list entry; other hero names ending in -man in the same passages (Aquaman, Sandman, Doll Man) are not where it peaks, and the opposite pole takes 'comic' in 'webcomic'.

484163.title: Punctuation closing a phrase after a name
484163.explanation: The unit fires on the punctuation mark itself, a full stop, comma or closing bracket, when it comes straight after a proper name or a number or letter label and really ends the sentence or phrase: "Eve is cast as Cora.", "loses again in Game 4.", "a prisoner, Conway.", "Danny shoots Saunders.", "Rustad,", "Drury, Kansas", the footnote marks "[C]" and "[N 2]", and a decimal comma in "2,5". It is a low-level reaction to the token and the capitalised word or figure just before it, strongest after a short flat statement ending in a name. Full stops that only mark an abbreviation, and punctuation after ordinary lower-case words, do not fire it; in the plot summaries it is weak and shows only on sentence-final stops after names ("Ed.", "Quint.", "Protocol 10.").

485646.title: Middle of the word "recognize", any language
485646.explanation: The unit fires on a piece in the middle or at the end of a word meaning "to recognize / recognizable", whatever the language: English recogn-ize, recogn-is-ably, German erk-enn-bar and er-ken-nt, Russian распоз-н-ать, French reconnaitrie-z, Chinese 认-不出 ("cannot recognize"). It reacts to the word itself, which is usually split into pieces, and the topic around it (heraldry, botany, literary criticism, a detective scene) does not matter. Whole-word "recognizes" in plot summaries fires too but at well under half strength, and a few look-alike spellings also set it off (Reconnai-s-sance, the name Koen-ig). Other words for knowing, seeing or identifying do not appear.

492572.title: The word "district" and its foreign spellings
492572.explanation: The unit reacts to the spelling of the word "district" itself, in any language: it peaks on the middle or final piece of the word as it is being spelled out, such as "rik" in German/Afrikaans "Distrikt" and "Distrikte", "kt" in "Distrikt" and Norwegian "formannskapsdistrikt", "rito" in Spanish and Portuguese "distrito", "rit" in "Distrital", and "ric" in a misspelt "distric attorney". In the English plot summaries it fires, more weakly, on the whole word "District" or "district", almost always in "district attorney". It is a word-form detector, not a meaning detector: other words for administrative areas (province, county, Kreis, municipality) do not trigger it, while a look-alike letter string such as "Bistrički" does.

494694.title: The "tox" stem in toxin/toxic words
494694.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the word piece that completes the stem "tox" ("ox" or "x" after "to", Russian "с" after "ток") inside words about poison, such as antitoxin, neurotoxins, cytotoxins, Toxoplasma, Ökotoxikologie, Toxics, интоксикация and токсический. It works across English, German and Russian and regardless of whether the passage is about venom, bacteria, chemistry or a place name; whole-word tokens "toxin" and "toxic" fire it at about half strength. Other words that begin with "to" but do not continue as "tox" (for example French "toit") do not fire it.

496912.title: Words "studies" (case studies) and "status"
496912.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself, in two main groups: the word "studies" right after "case" ("case studies" in marketing, sales and business-advice text), and the word "status" as an abstract noun ("status quo", "the status of a university college", "out-of-print status", "our status as"). A weaker third group is the word "unknown" used as a descriptor ("unknown length", "intentions unknown", "unknown medication"), with scattered faint hits on "option", "network", "circles" and "diner" that share no clear meaning. It is a word-level unit, not a topic unit: business or marketing text without these exact words does not fire it, and the groups are related only loosely, so there is no single idea beyond the particular words.

504290.title: End of names like Stoker, Coker, Gozer, Joker
504290.explanation: Fires on the last piece of a proper name that is spelled or sounds like '-oker', '-ocker' or '-ozer': C-oker (Coker College, Larry Coker, Cait Coker), St-oker (Bram Stoker, the Stoker Company, Stoker's Halt), Stock-er (Stocker Avenue, Mrs. Stocker, Ben Stocker, Charles William Stocker, and the Russian Сток-ер), Go-zer and Joker. It reacts to the marked token itself together with the letters just before it, not to meaning: the surrounding text ranges over colleges, a street address, a pesticide company, horror awards and film plots. All the top passages are capitalised names; other names ending in '-er' in the same passages (Peter, Snyder, Fowler) do not take the peak, and no common word of this shape, such as poker or broker, appears among them.

506907.title: Second piece completing a famous name: Biden, Trump, Ten
506907.explanation: This unit reacts to the marked token itself: the word-piece that completes a well-known fixed name. Most of the top firings are 'Biden' right after 'Joe', then 'Trump' (after 'Donald' or in 'Trump's Castle'), and 'Ten' in 'Big Ten' (the college sports conference); weaker cases are the same kind of completion in other names, 'ham' in 'Arkham', the X in 'SPX', and the middle syllable of 'YouTube' written in Korean. It is a spelling-level response to these particular name endings rather than to politics or sport as a topic: other presidents named in the same lists (Obama, Clinton, Bush) and the number ten used on its own do not appear at the peaks.

507250.title: Game-mechanic action words: battle, defeat, trade, arena
507250.explanation: Fires on words naming what players do in a game, mainly fighting and exchanging: "battle(s)", "defeating/defeated", "arena", "trade/trading", and to a lesser degree "completing" or "repair". It is strongest inside the Gameplay section of a video-game or board-game article, where the sentence is describing modes, rewards or how players obtain things ("by defeating enemies", "PvP arena modes", "trading them with friends"). The same words in ordinary story text (a plot summary where someone defeats a villain, trades petrol, or fights in a makeshift arena) fire only weakly, at about a third of the maximum, and other parts of game articles (release dates, developers, reception) do not fire.

511328.title: Completing the word "Superman" / "supermen"
511328.explanation: The unit reacts to the spelling of the marked token: it fires on the piece that completes a word begun with "Super", above all "man" or "men" in Superman / supermen, and on the same word in other scripts (Chinese 超人, Arabic سوبرمان). It fires for the comic-book hero, for a generic race of superior beings, for a song title, and even when the letters are an accident ("supermaneuverable"), so it follows the word form rather than the meaning. A weaker group is other "Super-" words (Superior, Superliga) and, loosely, Huron; when "Superman" is a single token, as in the plot summaries, it fires on the whole name at lower strength. Plain "man" or "men" without the "Super" prefix, and other hero names, do not appear.

515471.title: The words compose, composes, composition
515471.explanation: Fires on the word family compose / composes / composition / compositional itself, peaking on the token that carries the stem (composition, -poses, -itional). The meaning does not matter: it fires alike for the composition of a painting, of lighting, of a neighbourhood or of a metal, for someone who composes a ballad or a poem, and for someone who composes himself or herself after an upset. Other words about art, style, music or calming down do not appear at the peaks, so it reacts to the spelling of the word, not to a topic. In the plot summaries, which contain no such word, it fires only weakly (about half strength or less) on other Latin-derived abstract words such as existential, coexist, simultaneous, epilogue, mentally and discreetly, which are not the same idea.

517223.title: Function word right after a missing noun
517223.explanation: The unit fires on a small grammatical word (on, in, to, of, which, who, was, did, a, a comma) that arrives where a noun, name, number or date should have been: the text has a hole, usually because a term, ship name, measurement or date was stripped out, as in "formed a [gap] on", "summoned a [gap] on", "command of the [gap] in 1939", "backed by [gap] of wood", "Le [gap] a perdu", or the blanks in "I am a __ __ who". It reacts to the situation before the marked token (an article or preposition left hanging with nothing after it), not to the word itself, and it works in French as well as English. The same prepositions in complete, normal sentences fire only weakly, which is why the plot-summary sentences score low and share nothing clear.

523659.title: Continuation of a name or term starting with G
523659.explanation: The unit reacts to spelling, not meaning: it fires on the token that comes right after (or shortly after) a word or name beginning with the letter G, such as Graham Per-due, Giant Tiger, Graham Holland, G-index, G-numbers, GNU Privacy, G. Stanley, Gossyp-ium, Gamb-ela, Gigantopithec-us, glycosyl hydrol-ase, Gracefield is, gSOAP is, and Gotham City. The subjects are unrelated (chemists, shops, greyhounds, plants, enzymes, software, a fictional city); what they share is the G-initial word just before or containing the marked token. It does not fire on the G token itself, and words starting with 'Ge' (Georges, Georg, Geo-) drive the opposite pole instead.

525206.title: Reported opinion: "is X and should" modal
525206.explanation: Fires on the modal verb (overwhelmingly "should", less often could, will, would) that opens the second half of a reported opinion or claim of the form "someone believes / says / convinces him that X is [a judgment] and should ...". The first half states an assessment of a person or thing (is talented, is a rebel, is a big-shot, is antiquated, has a good brain) and the marked word starts the consequence or recommendation drawn from it. Weaker firings keep the same frame with another word starting the second predicate after "and" ("is not a king and would need", "is a warning beacon and not", "is trained and has"). A plain "should" in direct speech, a question or a main clause, without the preceding "that X is ... and" in someone's reported view, does not fit the pattern.

528763.title: "For the" openers and "in the main"
528763.explanation: Two related groups. The most common is the word "the" right after a sentence- or document-opening "For" ("For« the» Record", "For« the» first time in five years", "For« the» 1994-95 school year", "For« the» full list of settings"), with a weaker version on "the" after an opening "In" in plot summaries ("In« the» mid-1940s", "In« the» near future", "In« the» Fire Swamp"). The very strongest firings are on "main" completing the fixed phrase "in the main" (meaning 'mostly'). It responds to the marked token in that position, a capitalised opening preposition followed by "the", or the idiom's last word; "the" in the middle of a sentence or "main" as an ordinary adjective ("main road") does not appear among its firings.

529076.title: First ordinary word after a document's opening
529076.explanation: The unit fires at the very beginning of a text, on the second or third token: the first plain word that follows the opening item, which is usually a title or odd name ("Ju Dou takes", "Zyyg is", "CFFB is", "RTJ4 is", "8BC was"), a year or number ("1935. A", "1881. About", "68. The", "21-year-old") or a cut-off word fragment ("nnum, and", "dth between"). It is reacting to position, not meaning: the marked words are common function words or verbs (is, was, the, a, and, of, at, takes, -old) that carry no shared topic. The same words later in a document do not fire it, and in the plot summaries it shows only weakly, always in the first sentence.

529495.title: Sentence resuming after stray inserted text
529495.explanation: Fires on the word where a running sentence picks up again after something foreign has broken into it: a page number dropped mid-sentence or mid-word ("p. 43 request", "p. 191 hearts", "293 division", "220 little dwarf"), a marginal note or source citation in old chronicles ("Simon Dun. saith", "...deliuered to the French king. besieged", "Inquisitions taken. crowne"), or a picture caption pasted into the prose ("An Arabian Musician instruments", "photograph"). A weaker related group is words that sit out of their expected order or follow a broken join ("Prime Levi Minister", "middle immense room", "Beautiful very, picture this", "psidii. particularly"). It reacts to the disruption before the marked word, not to the word's meaning; the same words in clean, uninterrupted prose do not fire it, and in the plot summaries it only fires faintly on unrelated words.

534924.title: End of a clause relating two counterparts
534924.explanation: The unit fires on the comma, semicolon or small linking word ("in", "by", Japanese "に") that comes right after a statement has set two paired or opposed things against each other: No. 1 before No. 2, the city upon the country, men than women, the dwarf than the giant, the strong hunting the weak, east versus west, straight opposite of crooked, the front pre-dating the rear, alternating to direct current. What matters is the meaning of the text before the mark, a comparison, ordering or contrast in which the second member of the pair has just been named, and it works in English, Spanish and Japanese alike. Commas and semicolons after ordinary clauses with no such pair of counterparts do not fire it; in the plot summaries it is only weak, on sentences like "three of them ... the fourth," or "Volume Two ... Volume One."

539912.title: Last word of a fixed name: Secret Wars, Solomon Grundy
539912.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself when it completes a set, name-like phrase the model already recognises from its first word. The strongest cases are the "Wars" of Marvel's "Secret Wars" (as a title or section heading in comics articles) and the final "y" of "Solomon Grundy"; weaker ones are other completed titles and compounds such as "The Graveyard Book", "Grimm's Law", "Secret War(s)" in book titles, "Laguna Madre", "Delbarton", "Deathstroke" and "secret identity". There are two or three loose groups (phrases starting with "Secret", the name Solomon Grundy, other two-part titles and names), tied together by the closing piece of a familiar fixed name rather than by a topic. It does not fire on the first word of such names, on "wars", "book" or "law" used as ordinary nouns, or on other character names in the same lists.

543504.title: Kaiju and other genre-label words
543504.explanation: The unit fires most strongly on the last piece of the word "kaiju" ("Kai«ju»"), the Japanese giant-monster term, in monster film plots (Pacific Rim, Gamera, Godzilla, Destroy All Monsters) and in names such as Kaiju Big Battel. A weaker, looser second group is the word that completes or names another pop-culture genre or entertainment format: "escape room", "Squid Game", "board games", "zombie" and "zombie outbreak", "paranormal", "Jurassic Park", "electromagnetic pulse", "metahumans". It reacts to the token finishing such a genre or fantasy-concept label, not to monsters or action being described in ordinary words; plain "monster", "creature" or "Godzilla" are not at the peaks.

544109.title: Brief or one-off occurrences: briefly, appearance, spell
544109.explanation: The unit fires on words that mark a short, limited or single occasion of doing something: "briefly", "a brief appearance", "briefly appeared", "had a spell at", "thinking for a bit", "a heart-to-heart conversation", "an attempt", "repeated contact", "last at-bat", "the last time we were here", "often enough". It is strongest in career biographies (an actor made a brief appearance, a footballer or manager had a spell at a club) and in plot summaries where characters talk, kiss, reunite or fight briefly, or make an attempt. What matters is the sense of an episode measured by how short it was or how many times it happened; statements of large amounts (many, countless, over 200, a large number of) do not fire it and belong to the opposite pole.

550964.title: Completing a superhero-comics proper name
550964.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a well-known proper name from the DC or Marvel comics world: a character (Power Girl, Emma Frost, Lois Lane, Booster Gold, Nightwing, Batwing, Punisher, Psylocke, Darkseid, Lex Luthor, Barbara Gordon), an institution in that world (Xavier Institute, Daily Planet, Squadron Supreme) or occasionally a comics creator (John Romita). It reacts to the marked token itself, but only when the preceding word and the surrounding superhero context make it the second half of such a name; the first word of the name and the same words in ordinary text (a girl, an institute, a planet, a wing) do not trigger it. It is a name-recognition signal, not a reaction to any kind of scene or event.

553323.title: Small linking word right after a title or name
553323.explanation: The unit fires on a short linking word (in, and, to, by, for, the, 's, a dash) that comes immediately after a capitalised name or title, most often the subject of the article or a shortened or variant form of it ("Doctors in 2019", "the rival News to form", "Fly by Night", "Dignity for Disability", "East and West Peckham", "Computer and Video Games"). It is reacting to the position, not to the particular word: the point where a proper name either ends and the sentence resumes, or carries on into a longer multi-word title. It does not fire on the name itself, and the same small words in ordinary prose with no title or name just before them do not trigger it.

553609.title: Mythic or gothic monster-like names in genre stories
553609.explanation: The unit fires on the word piece at which a grand, myth-flavoured or gothic name becomes recognisable, almost always inside comic-book, science-fiction or fantasy text: Grend-el, Levi-athan, Fen-ris, Hyper-ion, A-riel, Excels-ior, Krak-oa, Pl-ut-onium, Else-where, and in the plot summaries Ark-ham again and again. A second, closely related group is ordinary words with the same dark or monstrous feel: garg-antuan, g-argo-yle, doppel-g-änger, a "shadow" demon, "reborn", a character changing his "face". It reacts to the marked token as the piece that completes such a name, in a setting of creatures, villains, ships and strange places; it does not fire on plain everyday names of people or towns, and the opposite pole takes technical labels such as C-3PO.

558309.title: DC Comics name parts; some physics terms
558309.explanation: Most strong firings land on a word inside a well-known DC Comics name or title, at the point where the name becomes recognisable: "Super" in "Legion of Super-Heroes" and "Legion of Super-Pets", "Earth" in "Crisis on Infinite Earths", and the character names "Damian" (Wayne), "Harley" (Quinn) and (Commissioner) "Gordon", plus a Kryptonian "meteorite". A second, smaller group is specialist theoretical and particle physics wording: the physicist "Thaler", "non-relativistic", "infinitely heavy quarks", "fixed target". The two groups do not obviously share one idea, so this is a mixed unit; the words "super" or "earth" in ordinary text are not shown firing, and the opposite pole of the neuron takes Marvel's Bruce Banner and game attributes like Strength.

559532.title: Last piece of a comic-book character name
559532.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes the name of a character or place from superhero comics (DC and Marvel), at the point where the name becomes recognisable: Captain Boomer"ang", Doctor "Spectrum", Mole "Man", Cyc"lops", Mister Sin"ister", Professor "Xavier", Doctor "Strange", Att"uma", Kat"ma" Tui, Aunt "May", Cat"woman", Red "Hood", and the planet O"a" of the Green Lantern Corps. The surrounding text is always about superheroes, their teams, villains or rosters, and the unit reacts to the finished name rather than to the word itself. It does not fire on the first piece of these names, and words like "man", "strange", "may" or "hood" in ordinary text outside a superhero setting should not set it off.

559572.title: Name of an invented city or country
559572.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes the name of a made-up place where a story is set: Steelport, Raccoon City, Calvard, New Granada, Zamunda, Freedonia, Tokyo-3, Panem, Metroville, Starling City, Bay City, Rohan, Florin, Arendelle, Blüdhaven, Gotham City. The name usually follows a phrase that introduces a setting, such as "the fictional city of", "the country of", "the kingdom of", "the nation of" or "the Republic of", and the peak falls on the last piece of the invented name or on "City". Real places named in the same passages (New York, Japan, Cape Town, New Zealand) and the names of fictional people or organisations do not trigger it.

565231.title: Animated versions of DC superhero comics
565231.explanation: The unit fires on the word "animated" (or "cartoon") when the text is about superhero comics characters and their screen adaptations, above all "Batman: The Animated Series", the "DC Animated Universe" and DC animated films; it reacts to what the surrounding text means, not just to the word. A second, related group is names tied to that same world in cast lists for the Batman Arkham games: the voice actors Kevin Conroy and Tara Strong, and the names Arkham, Wayne and Thomas (Wayne). The word "animated" used for an unrelated series earlier in the same passage (for example a British children's cartoon) does not set it off until a superhero or Batman title appears; one stray firing on "cosmology" does not fit.

568990.title: Codenames of comic-book and sci-fi villains
568990.explanation: Fires on the token that completes the codename of a costumed or alien character in superhero and science-fiction text, most often an enemy: the Borg, the Tattooed Man, Cheetah, Electro, the Celestial Toymaker, Parasite, Viper, Taskmaster, Black Manta, Hush, Mr. Freeze, Gorilla Grodd, the Scarecrow. It reacts to the name itself once the surrounding text has made clear it is a villain or super-powered alias, and a few hero aliases (Hawkeye, Firestorm, Huntress) also trigger it. Ordinary personal names in the same passages (Peter, Harry, Clark Kent, Picard) and plain descriptive words do not fire it.

573576.title: End of a song title or verse line
573576.explanation: Fires at the point where a short title-like or verse-like phrase is complete: on the last word of a song or album title ('River of Pain', 'Just Outside of Heaven', 'Bedtime for Democracy', 'Through the Iris', 'Black Heart Inertia') or on the closing quotation mark or bracket right after it, mostly in album articles and track listings. A second group is the end of a line of poetry or of odd, garbled text ('a legend of no one.', 'no Subway at the monastery.', 'cotton petals,'). It reacts to the position and to the figurative, title-style wording before it, not to any one token. Plain sentence endings and conjunctions in ordinary prose, as in the plot summaries, fire only weakly.

581933.title: Vampire lore: blood-drinking and feeding
581933.explanation: The unit fires inside text that is already about vampires, and peaks on the words that carry the vampire idea itself: "blood" after "drink" or "animal", "feed on", "craving for", "thirst", the middle of "vampire"/"vampirism", and the "quer" of the game title "Vampire: The Masquerade". It reacts to the meaning built up before the token (a vampire who drinks or abstains from blood) rather than to the word "blood" alone, so blood in a medical, war or crime passage should not trigger it. Outside vampire stories it fires only at about half strength, on dark night-creature figures: a man "dressed as a bat", "Bat" in Batcave/Batmobile, a masked outlaw "dressed entirely in black" and the word "vigilante".

588934.title: Bottom or walls of a vessel or container
588934.explanation: Fires on the word "bottom" (less often "sides", "lining", "double-walled", "skin", "lowest part") when it names the floor or inner wall of something that holds liquid or material: a pot, kettle, pan, tank, retort, boiler, cistern, pool, diffusion cell, silo, a dug-out boat or a ship's hull. The passages are practical descriptions - recipes, manuals, chemistry, engineering, how things are made - and often speak of something settling, sticking or lying at the bottom. It reacts to the marked word in that container sense, not to the opening of a container ("mouth" belongs to the opposite pole). In the plot summaries it is only weak (under half strength) and lands on villain names such as the Riddler, Lex Luthor and Mr. Freeze, which look unrelated to the main pattern.

594827.title: Last token completing a well-known proper name
594827.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a recognisable multi-part name, most often the surname of a famous person: Yoko On«o» (many times), Joseph Beu«ys», Earl of Lovel«ace», the C«usan», Barbara «Gordon», Tony «Stark». A second group is the closing word of a named thing: Third «Man» Records, Project «Row» Houses, «Wayne» Manor, Green «Goblin», Boph«ana». The strongest corpus cases lean heavily toward avant-garde art and music figures and labels, so the unit is reacting to the marked token as the end of a known name rather than to the meaning of the passage. It does not fire on the first part of a name, and a few weaker hits ('parents', the 'is' in Sionis) do not fit cleanly.

598347.title: Career civil, diplomatic and military service corps
598347.explanation: Fires inside the names of official state service bodies and the classes of people who staff them: 'career' before diplomats or civil servants, 'Service(s)' in Foreign Service or Civil Services, 'professional' firefighters, 'administrative' law judges, civil-service grades in Hindi and Chinese, and the names of army regiments (Cavalry, the Buffs, Kumaon, Infantry). It reacts to what the surrounding text means, namely government, diplomatic, military or police staffing, and peaks on the word that marks the corps or grade. In the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on police and army labels such as NYPD, Commissioner Gordon and 9th Infantry Division. Two strong hits do not fit (ventral 'tegmentum', the string 'number' in JavaScript), and everyday uses of 'career' or 'service' outside officialdom are not among the examples.

604262.title: Superhero and supervillain words
604262.explanation: The unit fires on the words "superhero", "supervillain" and their pieces ("superv", "ill", "heroes", "super" in "superhuman", and the Chinese "英雄" in "超級英雄"), mostly in the opening sentence of comic-book character articles and in plots about costumed heroes and villains. It reacts to the marked word itself and the idea behind it: a person with powers or a costumed secret identity. More weakly it fires on nearby ideas in the plot summaries: "heroism", donning a "costume", a "costumed vigilante", adopting an alias, gaining special abilities. Ordinary heroes, criminals or villains with no comic-book, powers or costume framing do not appear; one outlier is "also known as" introducing a psychic's nickname.

609893.title: Height measurements, plus unrelated Bosnian word pieces
609893.explanation: There is no single idea here; the passages fall into loose groups. The clearest group is how tall a body is: the unit peaks on the measure word or figure when a height is being stated or changed ("a height of five inches", "gained two inches", "over 4-foot-6", "6'2", "6'4\"", a horse that "stood 15 hands", bones growing longer, a vehicle's height). A second, unrelated group is the middle of the word Bosnian or Bosniak in English and German (Bos-n-ian, Bos-ni-aken), and a third is scattered words for a physical or chemical property (alkaline, quenched, positively charged). The film-plot sentences (a genetically engineered spider, Oscorp, Jurassic, billionaire) fire more weakly and fit none of these groups, so ordinary mentions of size or of other nationalities should not be expected to fire reliably.

617527.title: Null or existence test on a looked-up item
617527.explanation: The strongest group is source code inside an if-condition that tests whether a looked-up thing exists: the unit peaks on the compared value or operator in "!= null", "!= nil", "=== undefined", "% MAX != 0", "!== 'function'", "'form.submitted' in", or on the bracket closing a key lookup in "if (!obj[key])" and "if (!this.routes[verb])". A second group is mathematical prose where a just-named symbol is about to be defined, with the peak on the verb ("and ... denotes", "and ... are, respectively", "costA(X) for algorithm"). Much more weakly, in plot summaries it fires on the possessive "'s" after a person's name just before a relation word ("Walden's daughter", "Gavin's wife", "Grissom's mistress"). What the groups share is the point just after a reference to a named item where something is about to be stated or tested about it; ordinary assignments, function calls and comparisons that follow a parenthesised call or assignment do not show up.

621792.title: Modifier awaiting its fixed head noun (Russian decades)
621792.explanation: The unit fires on a modifier that is about to be completed by one highly predictable generic noun. By far the strongest case is the Russian case ending attached to a decade number («1940-х», «1990-х», «1970-е», «70-х»), usually after «в конце / с конца / в начале», just before «годов» or «годы» (years). The weaker English cases have the same shape: «hyoid» before bone, «pituitary» before gland, «Delaware» before River, and «Gotham» before City in the plot summaries. It does not fire on plain four-digit years such as «в 1995 году» or on the head noun itself; it reacts to the incomplete modifier, in anticipation of the word that follows.

622905.title: Where a name or title comes from
622905.explanation: A loose unit with no single trigger word. Its clearest group is sentences that say what a title or name is taken from or what a named thing essentially is: "The album's title is based on", "The name of the stable is inspired by", "was chosen to mean", "after the Tibetan Buddhist term drala", "borrows lines from the Dies Irae", and the article's own subject being named again in a defining sentence ("essential to black metal", "Aphrodite Urania", "Daivathaar as a channel of Lord Rama"). A second, weaker group in plot summaries is a character's showy signature object, costume or gesture: a spectacular stunt, enchanted Phoenix armor, dressing as superheroes or as a bat, Two-Face's coin or die, a penguin army. Ordinary mentions of titles or names with no statement of origin or identity, and plain action sentences without an emblematic prop, do not stand out, but the two groups are only loosely tied and the pattern is not sharp.

623466.title: Possessive ending after a group or institution
623466.explanation: The unit fires on the possessive marker, 's or the bare apostrophe after a plural, at the point where a noun has just been turned into an owner and the thing owned is about to be named: the second years' childhood, the municipalities' proposals, the Old Boys' dinner, the police's lack of effort, the organization's dealings, the United Underworld's HQ. The strongest cases follow a group, a plural or an institution; possessives after one person's name (Peter's, Wickham's, Batman's) fire only weakly, and the Danish genitive ending in Techplatform«enes» does the same job. A weaker, looser group is other small linking words that attach what follows to what came before (out «of» business, «into» his design, in «its» report, guide two criminals «through»). In these passages the apostrophe is marked only where it signals possession.

640973.title: Games, sport and playful pretending being described
640973.explanation: The unit reacts to what the text before the marked token means, not to a particular word: it fires when a game, sport or piece of play is being described. The strongest cases are the invention of basketball by James Naismith, ancient ball and board games (the Maya and Aztec ball game, patolli), and people playing, racing, chasing each other, pretending or acting something out (children pretending to be ghosts, captives made to act out a play, a carnival stunt team, a fair). In the plot summaries it fires more weakly on disguises, tricks and hobbies, which share the pretending side. It is loose: several strong passages (Karbala, a cast list, a suicide pact, someone searching for friends) have no game or play in them, so ordinary action or violence without play can also set it off at lower strength.

643521.title: Last token of a film star's name
643521.explanation: The unit fires mostly on the token that completes the name of a well-known screen actor given in brackets after a character in a film plot: Warren Beatty, Ann-Margret, Marilyn Monroe, Ann Blyth, George Peppard, Christian Bale, Rita Hayworth, Ginger Rogers. It reacts to the marked token itself, at the moment a famous name becomes recognisable, and more weakly to the end of other familiar names and set compounds (Metropolis, Peter Parker, Quesada, Gotham, Lego, Summerlin Road, five-million-dollar, Idaho airport) and to film-making words such as "filmed" and "the camera". It does not fire on the character names in the same sentences or on the first part of the actor's name, and the non-actor cases (a number in code, "several seasons") do not fit one idea cleanly.

649831.title: Mid-phrase link inside a trailing explanatory clause
649831.explanation: This unit has no single word or topic; the pattern is loose and grammatical. It fires late in a long sentence, a few words into a trailing clause that gives the means, reason or detail of what was just stated ("as his forearms and hands have been replaced", "as President Patil gave her assent to", "by sending assassins to kill", "by naming him Prince of", "by threatening to divorce", "through raising funds for", "for there was no light to be seen"), on the linking word or verb that settles how the phrase will be completed: to, of, for, on, by, off, have, exactly, named, kill, divorce, son, seen. A few peaks are continuations of a date or number instead ("Christmas Eve, 1958", "the 10th edition", "1986"), which do not fit as well. The same small words at the start of a sentence or in a short main clause do not fire it, and the firings in the plot summaries are weak.

658370.title: Qualifier word inside a label for a person
658370.explanation: The unit fires part-way through a noun phrase that says what kind of person someone is, on the word giving their field, type or affiliation just before the role noun arrives: "open-wheel racing team manager", "stagecoach driver", "one-day specialist", "American television executive producer / actor", "film studio ... executive", "floating singles buyers", "computer programmer", "fashion-forward co-workers", "Vichy French and German officials", "Gotham City police officer". A second, related group is people defined by a place, a condition or a habit: the demonym "Villemomblois", "milonguera" (a woman tango dancer), "locals at casinos", "the person accessing the system", and three times "an individual with an autosomal recessive disorder". The same words used without labelling a person do not seem to be what drives it: in the genetics passages "disorder" occurs several times but the peak is always the one in "an individual with an autosomal recessive disorder". The pattern is fairly loose, and in the plot summaries it is weak, with a few peaks on plain function words ("and", "a").

674436.title: Mid-phrase in stock contrast or explaining expressions
674436.explanation: This unit fires part-way through a stock expression in explanatory prose, at a word after which the rest of the phrase is largely fixed. One group is the second half of a contrast or distinction: "win or lose", "long and short", "as distinct from", "in contrast to", "used to distinguish", "the different", "no longer", "any more". A second group is verbs and connectives that say what something shows: "meant to demonstrate", "suggest that", "to point out how", "a section that conveys". It reacts to the position inside such a construction rather than to a topic or a particular word (subjects range from biology to board games to code), the pattern is loose, and in plot summaries it is weak and scattered over mid-phrase words such as "hold ... to ransom" or "watch the world burn"; plain narration, names and sentence openings do not set it off.

675471.title: Inside a believed, assumed or supposed claim
675471.explanation: The unit fires on small linking words (is, be, a, that, the, it, indeed) in the middle of a clause that states what someone believes, assumes, claims or supposes to be the case, or a condition under which something holds, usually where the text is weighing that against what is really so: "the assumption that the person is in fact a terrorist", "mistakenly believes to be a shoe factory", "certain that Light is Kira", "believing her to be the daughter", "found to be a fake", "if the graph indeed admits a perfect clustering", "suppose we claim that n is prime", values "offset from" the true value. It is not tied to any one word and is strongest in mathematical or statistical explanations that set up correct versus incorrect cases, then in plots about mistaken belief, disguise or fakes. Plain narration of events does not fire it, and the moment a truth is actually proved or revealed (innocent, exonerated, turns out, true) belongs to the opposite pole; the pattern is loose and the weaker passages fit it only roughly.

679340.title: Last token completing a famous proper name
679340.explanation: The unit fires on the token that completes a well-known multi-part name, at the moment the name becomes recognisable: "Rand" in Ayn Rand, "Stark" in Tony Stark (also in Chinese), "Wayne" in Bruce Wayne, "Queen" in Oliver Queen, "Science" in Christian Science, and the endings of place names such as Mystic Falls, Plano and Shreveport, plus Menendez and Rango. The names fall into a few groups: Ayn Rand and her individualist ideas (including "man must act for his own self-interest"), rich businessmen who are secretly heroes (Stark, Wayne, Queen), Christian Science, and some American towns; in the plot summaries it is almost entirely the first mention of Bruce Wayne or Tony Stark. It does not fire on the hero name Batman or Iron Man, on the first half of the name, or on most other names in the same passages (actors, other characters); a couple of code hits ("(env", "sails") do not fit.

691885.title: Triggering event in a general rule clause
691885.explanation: Fires on the verb or event word inside a short clause that names the occasion or the set of cases to which a general, habitual or conditional statement applies: "every child he met", "every time we come in", "all she hears", "all the petitions that were presented", "any individuals encountered", "matter that fell into", "when tossed", "once struck", "when lit", "after they are defeated", "if anyone is caught", "anything hit by", "on contact with water", "in a power failure". The clause is usually attached to every / all / any / each / whenever / when / if, and the marked word is the happening that sets off the rule, not the main action. It reacts to that role rather than to any particular word, so the same verbs narrating a single one-off event in the main line of a story do not fire, and neither do plain statements of how many per day or year (those belong to the opposite pole).

694663.title: Proper name carrying a definite article
694663.explanation: Fires as a name that takes a definite article is being finished or has just been finished and stands alone as the whole noun phrase: 'The Comoros,', 'the Memorial,', 'the Fruska Gora', 'the Saarland', 'the Arran at', 'the Skela,', 'The Lalla recovered', 'The Chalhoub Group is', 'the Jugoslavs', 'The Lord Carew', French 'du Roeulx', Portuguese 'do Bom Sucesso', Arabic al-Qustantiniyya, and in plots 'the Penguin', 'the Pride Lands', 'the Red Hood', 'the Scarecrow forces'. The peak falls on the last piece of the name or on the comma, verb or preposition right after it, so it is about the situation (an article-marked name now complete), not one word; common nouns used the same way ('the downtown', 'the rhinotomy as') also trigger it. It does not fire when the name is followed by a generic class word such as unit, division, neighborhood, area or program (that is the opposite pole), and names without an article are weak.

698739.title: Superheroes: the word and superhero names
698739.explanation: The unit fires when the text invokes the idea of a costumed comic-book superhero. Most strongly it reacts to the marked word itself: "superhero", "superheroes", "heroes" for hire, "super"-powers, or a piece of superhero vocabulary such as Supergirl, Kryptonite, "Holy ..., Batman!" and "Truth, Justice and the American Way". More weakly it fires on the civilian name of a well-known superhero at the start of a plot (Bruce Wayne, Peter Parker) and on a sentence listing newly gained powers or public acts of heroism. It does not fire on ordinary fighting, bravery or self-defence without the superhero frame (that is what the opposite pole shows), and "hero" in a plain sense is only a weak trigger.

699945.title: Word opening a two-sided relation (from X to Y)
699945.explanation: The unit fires on the verb or preposition that opens a relation between two things, just before those two things are named: "connections from one brain area to another", "the ratio of ... to", "the vector pointing from ... to", "compare X with", "comparing it to", "a USB stick that links politicians to the mafia", "connect him to", "trade produce for petrol", "StringUtils.join(". It reacts to what the marked word sets up (a first item that will be paired, linked, compared, moved or exchanged with a second one through a following to/with/for), not to any single word, and it also works in code, French and Arabic. In the plot summaries it is weaker and looser, landing on action verbs that carry something to a target ("bring her to", "drops bombs onto", "inject the shark with", "uses his last two bullets to"). An ordinary "from" or "of" that only gives a source or possession, with no second term expected, does not appear among the strong firings.

704899.title: End of a scene-setting opening phrase
704899.explanation: The unit fires on the last token of a short framing phrase that opens a clause and says in which case, time or place the coming statement holds: "In the latter case", "in others", "In a stricter sense", "In such cases", "In civil matters", "prior to then", "In the late 1980s", "In mediaeval England", "On a winter's day", "In the present day", "In Florence,", "There,", and the Chinese equivalent of "in muscle cells". It marks the point where the frame is complete and the main clause with its subject is about to start, so it is driven by sentence structure and what comes next rather than by any particular word; the strongest cases are contrast frames in expository prose (in some cases ... in others), the weaker ones time and place openers in plot summaries. The same words inside a clause, or "which/where" starting a defining relative clause ("a problem where", "for which"), do not trigger it.

707580.title: Point where a word is missing or wrong
707580.explanation: Fires on the token that shows the text has just gone wrong: a word has been dropped or garbled, and the marked token is the first one that does not fit what came before. Typical cases are a missing preposition ('is in love Musa Bhai', 'falls in love a girl', 'relationship Herbert Hoover', 'serious interest Uqab', 'five years the events'), a missing article or noun ('reputation as feisty customer', 'pop rock fronted by'), a bracket that is never closed ('(Noah Berry, Sr. tells', '(now known as Myanmar in 1941'), or a wrong word or stray comma ('all beggars all liable', 'law of aspects:', 'far on, the breeze'). It reacts to the broken grammar, not to any particular word or subject: the same words in a correctly formed sentence do not set it off, and the clean plot summaries barely trigger it (at most a fifth of its maximum, on slightly awkward phrasing).

714976.title: The verb "ends" / "ended" / "end"
714976.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: the word "end" in its verb forms ("ends", "ended", "end") and occasionally as a noun ("an end to speculation"). It fires whatever the sense: something finishing ("the trip ends suddenly", "the conference ended with"), someone stopping something ("NSA ends the project", "Elsa ends the winter", "which ended his coaching career"), the idiom "ends up" ("ends up delirious in a Budapest hospital", "ended up with him spending"), and even code comments ("assume that it ends in _id"). Other words for the close of events such as "finally", and words for beginning such as "start", do not fire it; those belong to the opposite pole.

715962.title: Connector opening a new clause or argument
715962.explanation: Two related groups. In prose it fires on the word that opens a subordinate clause after a verb, noun or comparison: 'that' (recommended that, to prove that, reminds us that, discovers that, unaware that, in the hope that), 'what' after a comparison (twice what, different from what it was, the reverse to what it is, dropped from what it had been), and more weakly because, if, which, when and as. In Python code it fires on the comma (or '={},') that closes one keyword argument when another name=value argument follows, as in 'status_code=response.status_code, response=response, error_map=error_map' or 'instance=None, owner=None'. What the two share is a boundary token after which a new self-contained clause or argument begins; the unit reacts to the marked token in that position, not to subject matter. Relative pronouns that follow a preposition (into whose, by whom, to whichever) do not fire it.

735851.title: City government: municipal bodies, councils, mayors, sewers
735851.explanation: The unit fires when the text is about local, city-level government and its public works. It peaks on the words themselves ('Municipal' in Bureau of Municipal Research or Municipal Corporation, 'municipal pier', 'Sewerage and Water Board', 'sewers', 'Department of Water and Power', 'councilman', 'mayoral') and, just as strongly, on the year or the person's name in a sentence telling a mayor's or city councillor's career ('elected to the City Council in 2000', 'Lord Mayor since 2006', 'a motion in 1964 to ban smoking in the council chamber', 'In 2010, Fennell was elected to her fourth term'). So it reacts to the meaning of what came before, not to dates as such: years and names elsewhere do not fire it, and the examples are all town or city administration rather than national politics. In the plot summaries it is much weaker and mostly lands on sewers under the city.

738215.title: Wrestling and superhero titles, codenames, hero talk
738215.explanation: The unit fires inside professional-wrestling and comic-book superhero writing, on the opening or middle word of a branded title or codename as it is being spelled out: championship names ("TNA World Heavyweight Champion", "World Tag Team Championship", "NXT UK Tag Team Champions", "Campeonatos de Parejas", "IWGP Heavyweight Championship"), team names ("Team 3D", "Secret Society", "Secret Avengers") and hero or villain aliases ("Boy of Steel", "Captain America", "Green Goblin", "Doctor Victor Fries"). A second, related group in superhero plots is the stock phrase about taking up the hero role: "using his abilities to fight crime", "use their powers to help people", "fights alongside", "resume his vigilantism". The same words in ordinary text (a real sports "World Cup", a real doctor or captain, "to" before an everyday verb) do not fire it; the wrestling or costumed-hero setting is what matters.

760600.title: Particle opening a limit phrase: up to, down to
760600.explanation: The unit fires on a small directional word (up, down, back, out, round, into) at the moment it starts a phrase that says how far something reaches, and it is strongest when the reach is in time: 'in use by freight up until 1955', 'retained this position up to 1934', 'continued to exist down to the present day', 'traced back to the late seventeenth century', 'out to a water depth of 200 m'. It reacts to the marked particle together with the preceding statement of something lasting or extending, just before the end point is named. Weaker firings are looser relatives: plain movement particles (down the sink drain, down an elevator shaft, out of a trust fund, upstate) and 'to'/'for' giving a final extent (beat him to near-death, tortures him to death, to his doom, for the rest of your life). It does not fire on the start point of a span; the opposite pole of the neuron responds to 'From'.

769190.title: About to name a job, post or office
769190.explanation: The unit fires at the point where a person's job or post is about to be named: on "as" (or the next small word) after "work", "job", "hired", "moonlighting", "working", and on the Chinese verb 任 / 擔任 ("serve as") just before a rank or position. A second, related group is the middle of the name of an office, department or institutional body ("Director for Research", "Data Monitoring Committee", "Research Library and Collection", 製片, 출판부 "press", 標本館 "herbarium"). It reacts to what is coming next (a role or unit name), not to the marked word itself; an ordinary "as" or "the" outside an employment or appointment setting does not fire, and a few weaker passages ("In 2005", "calling the police") fit only loosely.

793207.title: Midway through a predictable fixed name or number
793207.explanation: The unit fires partway through a set expression whose remainder is close to certain: inside an institution's name (Stanford «Graduate» School, Center for «Advanced» Study, Wharton School «of» the University), inside a year (19«9»1, 20«1»7), inside a code identifier («sim»base, self«.security»_level), or on the opening piece of a known name (Ark-ham, Lex-Corp, Los Angeles, Sergeant James Gordon). It is reacting to what is about to come next, not to the marked token, which varies widely; very often the completion has already appeared earlier in the same document. Stock openers (Located in, According to) and a figure just before its unit (260 million kyats, was 12 guineas) fit more loosely. The peak is never on the last word of the name, and the pattern is a loose family rather than one clean idea.

795211.title: The word "District" itself
795211.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token: the word "District" or "district(s)", strongest when it is capitalised and opens a heading, category line or list entry in an article about local government areas ("Districts of England", "District result maps", "District Headquarter", "District municipalities in Turkey"). It fires nearly as hard for the same word inside fixed names and titles such as "District Attorney", "District of Columbia", "District Heights", "District 11" and "district leader", and a little for the look-alike word "distribution". Other words for areas (ward, county, parish, borough, region) in the same texts do not set it off, and the few weak firings on unrelated tokens (a table bar in an electoral-district article, parts of personal names) look like noise.

795785.title: Linking verb before the predicate in formulaic prose
795785.explanation: Fires most often on a linking or helper verb - "is", "was", "be", "being", "been", and the Hindi verb stem "kar" (do) - at the point where a clause has named its subject and the predicate, usually a passive such as "marked by", "headed", "dumped", "examined" or "provided", is about to follow. It is strongest in dry, repetitive descriptive writing that keeps reusing one sentence frame, such as lists of district borders ("whose boundary is marked by ...") or a column-by-column account of a newspaper page. A minority of the top passages do not fit this: hits inside labels, headings and code ("WORM_SOBER", "jsb.imports", "RULE XVII.", "Suggestions for Reading", "Footnote 8 re source"), so the pattern is partly a loose one about a hinge token in boilerplate text rather than one clear idea. It does not respond to story content; in plot summaries it is weak and falls on similar mid-clause hinge words ("son", "suspect", "two", "is", "been").

805859.title: Link just before a hero's teammate is named
805859.explanation: The unit fires on the comma, "and", "as", "of", "by", "with", slash or bracket that comes right after one member of a heroic group has been named and just before another good-side character is named: the next Straw Hat, Pandava brother, Ninja Turtle, member of Naruto's team, companion of Jon or Sam, or the person behind Robin ("Robin (Tim Drake", "the current Robin, Tim Drake", "predecessor, Dick Grayson"). It is reacting to what is about to come (the name of a hero, sidekick, ally or protégé), not to the punctuation mark itself, and it is strongest in ensemble adventure stories from anime, comics and fantasy. The same link words before a villain's name ("at the hands of Lord Voldemort", "run by the evil Dr. Noah") do not fire it; those belong to the opposite pole, and ordinary commas in lists of things or places do not fire it either.

809845.title: Preposition before a place in space stories
809845.explanation: Fires on a small linking word (from, to, at, in, of, for, near, toward, around, by, or Chinese 回到 'return to') in science-fiction and adventure plot summaries, at the point where a named place or body is about to be given: Earth, the Moon, Mars, the Sun, Jupiter, a space station, a faraway country, a fictional base or institution. It is strongest when the sentence describes travel, launch, return or a battle located relative to a planet or other setting-defining place, and in space/anime works such as Doraemon, Star Trek, Gundam and Space: 1999 (it also fires a little on the name Doraemon and on dates in those articles). The same prepositions in ordinary non-fiction prose, or before the titles of fantasy book series, do not fire it.

811736.title: Midway through a fixed official name or title
811736.explanation: The unit fires partway through a set name of an office, institution, district or class, on the piece that comes just before a highly predictable ending: "State" in "Virginia State Senator", "Maryland State Senator", "77 state deputies" and "D.C. Statehood"; "of" in "American College of Surgeons"; "Black" in "Blackgate Penitentiary" and "Black Mask"; "White" in "White House"; and the first digit of a numbered designation ("21st Ward Alderman", "4ª Região" of a federal court, "6A", "12-member", "1983–1987" term of a governor). It is reacting to what is about to come next, the rest of a stock compound name, and most cases are political, legal, professional or prison bodies. A few peaks do not fit well (a quote mark before an XML tag name in code, a Hindi word fragment, the middle of the name "Khary", "DC" in a film title), so the pattern is a loose family rather than one clean idea; ordinary free-standing uses of these words or digits outside a set name are not among the strong firings.

813270.title: Names inside writing about video games
813270.explanation: The unit fires inside encyclopedia-style or news text about video games, on a piece of a name or label belonging to that world: a developer or staff member being credited ("brothers Joe and Bob Johnson", "game director Tim Schafer", "art director Derek Sakai", "French outfit Arkane Studios", "indie developer"), a platform or series title ("Wii U game", "Nintendo 64 port", "Fire Emblem", "Saints Row games", "Uncharted titles", "Gone Home"), or an industry term ("third-party", "single-player"). In the plot summaries it fires mostly in the Arkham video-game summaries, on franchise names in cast and setting descriptions (Joker, Batman, Arkham, Batcave), and also on "Bat" in Batgirl in two films. What matters is the game-article setting rather than the particular word; the same names in an ordinary film plot fire less, and one geometry passage ("pentagonal antiprisms") is an unexplained outlier.

813674.title: Muppets, He-Man and tokusatsu franchise character rosters
813674.explanation: The unit reacts to the surrounding subject, not to the marked token: it fires inside text about children's character franchises built on puppets, toys or costumed heroes, above all the Muppets and Jim Henson productions, then He-Man / Masters of the Universe and Japanese Kamen Rider / Super Sentai shows. The peak falls on a small linking word or comma ("of", "by", "for", "as", "such", "and", ",") or on the first letter "G" of a name (Gaim, Gwildor, Garo), at the point where a franchise character, performer or series title is about to be named or has just begun. In the plot summaries it fires more weakly in rosters of named heroes and villains (Nightwing, Robin, Mad Hatter, Clayface, the Joker). Text about newspaper comic strips and cartoonists does not fire it (that is the opposite pole), and ordinary plot narration without such a franchise cast stays quiet.

819099.title: Start of a known name or standard figure
819099.explanation: Fires where a specific, memorised item is being filled in, usually on its first piece or on the word just before it. One group is names of actors, characters and places: «Bruce» McGill (twice), 肖恩·托布 in a cast list, «James» Gordon, «Spider»-Man, «Phantom» Zone, «Cop»acabana, "district «attorney»" before Harvey Dent, "«Captain»" before Ellen Yindel, "his «daughter»," before Barbara Gordon. A second group is text about streaming, apps and devices, where it fires just before a stock number or string: "free «»7-day trial", "for «»60 days", "within «»48 hours", "68 million households «had» watched", «Chrom»ecast, model number GD«9»00, and codec or header strings in code. Plain narrative words with no fixed, recallable continuation do not trigger it; the two groups share only this 'specific known fact coming' quality, so the pattern is loose.

819222.title: The token "cloud", weather or computing
819222.explanation: The unit reacts to the word "cloud" itself, whatever it means: Amazon service names (CloudWatch, CloudTrail, CloudFront), weather and meteorology ("low cloud", "cloud base", "cloudless sky", "clouding", "cloud flying") and names such as "Cloud Nine" or the "Cloudburst" device. It usually fires when "cloud" is the first part of a compound or name. Much weaker and looser firings fall on the first piece of other compounds or split words ("load" shedding, "land" banking, "instance"_id, "crow"'s nest, "life"boat, "life" form, "arc" reactor, "mort"ally, "Mour"ning); these have no shared meaning. It does not fire on sky, rain or computing text that lacks the word "cloud".

824648.title: Slot just before a known character's name
824648.explanation: The unit fires at the point where a familiar supporting character of a well-known story is about to be named: the comma or last syllable after a role phrase ("his butler," before Alfred Pennyworth, "Lady Tremaine's cat," before Lucifer, "his girlfriend and downstairs neighbor," before Musette, "Cat burglar" before Selina Kyle), the verb "played" or "portrayed" before a role (Catwoman, Bombalurina), or the "and" joining a fixed pair of names (Firmin and Andre, John and Mary Grayson). It is reacting to what comes next, a predictable name, rather than to the marked token itself, and cats, butlers and the Paris opera and bohemian stories recur. Ordinary commas, "and" or "played" that do not lead into such a name do not fire it; a few weaker passages ("when I go shopping", "due to", "Tesla") do not fit.

825743.title: First piece of a predictable name, often comics
825743.explanation: The unit fires on a token that opens a name or term whose continuation is easy to guess, so it looks forward to what comes next rather than back at a meaning. There are two groups. The larger one is the word "the" (also "del", a colon in a title, or "returning") standing right before a named comic-book character, team or title in text about DC superhero comics: the Penguin, the Riddler, the Joker, the Cheetah, the Legion of Super-Heroes, the Lost Kingdom, the Cowl, the DC Extended Universe. The smaller but strongest group is a word-opening fragment about to be completed: " pun" (punas, puniques, Punisch), " Death" (Deathstroke), " pert" (pertencente). An ordinary "the" before a common noun outside this kind of name-heavy text does not fire it strongly, and the two groups are only loosely tied together.

826562.title: About to name a superhero-franchise supporting character
826562.explanation: The unit fires inside text about superhero comics and similar fan franchises (Captain America, Wonder Woman, DC and Marvel, Batman, also Doctor Who and Sailor Moon) at the point where a known character of that universe is about to be named or has only just begun to be named. The marked token itself varies: a rank or title (Col., Director, Commander, Dr., Lady), a first name or name fragment (Steve Trevor, Barbara Gordon, Tony Zucco, 'Jim', Dionysus), or a linking word right before the name (with, of, as, a comma), and occasionally a date or the word 'series' in the same kind of article. So it is driven by the surrounding franchise context and the expectation of a cast name, not by a particular word. The same sentence shapes in other settings do not fire it; the opposite pole of the neuron takes the equivalent spots in Buffy, Angel and Lost articles.

826801.title: Who invented, designed or developed something
826801.explanation: Fires where the text credits a scientist, doctor or inventor with making something: a device, virus, cure, drug, robot, algorithm or creature. The peak usually sits on the small linking word just before the maker's name or the made thing ("designed by", "created by Dr.", "invented in 1962 by", "grandson of the original Dr. Frankenstein"), or on the word naming the role or act itself ("inventor", "physicist", "discovered", "developing", "develop", "create"). It reacts to the meaning of the preceding text (an invention or research project and its originator), not to a particular spelling; plain "by" or "of" without an invention, science or creator context does not fire it. A few strong passages fit only loosely (a character name in a Chinese zombie-virus plot, "former head of the Soviet Psychic Corps", "research, development, test").

827221.title: Just before a canonical comic-lore name completes
827221.explanation: The unit fires on a small linking word or first name-piece (the, in, of, to, 's, "Central", "Ar") at the moment a well-known fictional-universe term is about to be completed, so it reacts to what comes next rather than to the marked token. The strongest cases are DC Comics and space-fiction lore: "the Central [Power Battery] on Oa", "sentenced to the [Phantom Zone]", "imprisoned him in [the Lost Sector]", "Scarecrow's [fear toxin]", "mayor of [Gotham City]", "center of the [galaxy]", "neutron [bomb/missiles]". A weaker second group is ordinary stock phrases about to finish ("plunged in [thought]", "plunged into deep [depression]", "uttered through [his teeth]"). The same linking words in plain text with no predictable named place, object or set phrase following do not fire it.

827593.title: Slot just before a character or director name
827593.explanation: Fires on the linking word or punctuation mark that comes right before a specific name is given: 'cast as', 'reprises his role as', 'stars ... as', 'directed by', 'called', 'named', 'the story of', 'vampire hunter', 'their leader', or a bracket, comma or slash that opens onto a character's name. It is anticipating the name, not reacting to the marked token itself, and the setting is almost always writing about action, superhero, comic or manga franchises (Blade above all, then the Punisher, Daredevil, Star Wars, Akira, Joker, Azrael, Red Hood). It does not fire on the name itself, nor on 'as' or 'by' in ordinary prose where no name is due; the same slot in some other story worlds goes to the opposite pole, so which franchise is involved also seems to matter.

829494.title: Midway through a multi-part name or title
829494.explanation: The unit fires at a point partway through a specific multi-part name, where the rest of the name is still to come and is fairly predictable: inside technical compound names (Fluorine-1«8» Labelled, 68Ga-PS«MA» PET, [12«]»crown-4), at the colon or first half of a title with a subtitle (Ghostbusters«:» Afterlife, Batman«:» Nightwalker, Blade« Runner»: Black Lotus, Looney T«unes» Super Stars), inside a person's name (Ra's «al» Ghul, «Toy» Newkirk), and at the comma, bracket or word that introduces a name about to be given ("his mother«,» Penny", "the« mineral» Lapis lazuli", "pygmy tarsier« (»Tarsius").
