It reacts to what is about to come rather than to the marked token itself, which varies from digits to punctuation to small words. The strongest passages are chemistry and nuclear-medicine names, the weaker ones film titles, cast lists and award categories; ordinary commas, colons and "of" that are not leading into or sitting inside a proper name or title do not appear. The grouping is loose: it is one position (inside or just before a named thing) more than one subject.

829722.title: Just before a known character is named
829722.explanation: The unit fires on the word or punctuation mark that sits right before a specific person is about to be named, after the text has set up who that person is by role or relationship: a job title ("district attorney" before Harvey Dent, "Deputy U.S. Marshal" before Samuel Gerard, "Detective" before Arbogast), a linking word ("as" before Harvey Bullock, "from" or "by" before mobster Sal Maroni, "married to", "estate of", "killer of"), or a comma, slash or bracket opening the name ("his parents, Thomas and Martha Wayne", "Batman's father, Dr. Thomas Wayne", "Thomas Wayne / Batman"). A related weaker group is backstory clauses that tie one character to another ("whom he once tried to assassinate", "a man her father once wanted", "whom Bowden defended"). It reacts to what is coming next, not to the marked token, and is strongest in crime and Batman material with lawmen, mobsters and relatives; the same small words ("of", "as", a comma) in places where no character name is due do not set it off, and neither does the name itself once it has been written.

832275.title: Boston places and Boston sports teams
832275.explanation: The unit fires when the text is about Boston and its surroundings: Fenway Park, the Boston Marathon course, Harvard and Harvard Square, Roxbury, the South End and North End, and Boston teams (Red Sox, Patriots, Celtics, Bruins). The peak usually falls on a small linking word next to a local place or team name ("Fenway Park in", "Brady and the", "between Harvard and", "Center at", "Boston's"), where a Boston-area name is in view or about to follow, and it works in Korean and Chinese too (inside the words for Boston Red Sox). It is weaker for Major League Baseball in general and for other "Sox" teams, and in the plot summaries it fires only faintly, mostly on "Red" in names like Red Hood and on the first name Thomas. Baseball or city text about other places (New York, San Francisco Giants) belongs to the opposite pole and does not fire it.

832905.title: Linking word just before a specific name
832905.explanation: No sharp single idea, but there is a loose pattern: the unit fires on a small connecting token (of, the, as, at, de, to, under, atop, a comma, a hyphen, a list number) or part-way through a term, at the point where a specific named thing or place is about to be given or completed: "such as" + product names, "the island of" + Minicoy, "Château de" + Muzot, "one of the" + Seven Basic Tools, Anopheles + funestus, Tukey + 's procedure. In the plot summaries the same slot is the location of a scene: "the abandoned" + Arkham Asylum or World's Fair, "to" + an abandoned amusement park, "a cavern under" + Wayne Manor, "the ruins of" + an orphanage, "atop" + the police car. It reacts to the expectation of the coming name or site, not to the meaning of the marked word, and many passages are encyclopedic descriptions of places (Maldives, Fiji, Kenya) or of technical methods; the same function words in ordinary narrative that are not leading into a named place or term do not show up.

833097.title: Link word before a named label or place
833097.explanation: It fires on a small linking token (at, in, by, of, and, the, a comma, an opening bracket, 'label', 'called') at the point where a specific proper name is about to be supplied: a record label in a discography ('(Columbia, 1956)', '(Blue Note', 'the label Tompkins Square', 'the Topic and Gael-linn labels', 'produced by Orrin Keepnews'), the town of a company or hospital ('The Edison Company at Orange', 'his hospital in Lambaréné'), or a named building or district ('the building called Wayne Manor', 'live at Wayne Manor', 'under Wayne Tower', Blackgate, Backport, 'the abandoned Arctic exhibit'). The strongest cases sit in historical writing about jazz and folk recordings and about early telegraph, telephone and electrical work ('advanced on the wire', 'cables de telégrafo'), often with New York nearby. The pattern is loose rather than one word or one topic: a few peaks in source code ('h :=', 'offset < 0') and one at a sentence end do not fit it.

836639.title: Lone first letter V (or R) of a word
836639.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself: a single initial letter, almost always "V"/"v" and sometimes "R", that has been split off as the first piece of a longer word or name whose rest has not yet been read (Varna, Varsity, Vogue, vials, Vittoria, venerated, Verte, vivacious, Vandyck, Voodoo; Rann-Thanagar, Riddler). In the plot summaries this is the "R" of "the Riddler" and "Ra's al Ghul" and the "V" of "Ventriloquist", usually inside a list of villains. The meaning of the surrounding text does not matter (roads, songs, antivenom, church music all work), and not every such letter fires it: the opposite pole takes other "R" starts such as Rancor and R2. A few weaker firings do not fit, on "level"/"-floor" after a number (6 level parking lot, seven-floor office tower), "pursue" and "Fire" of Firefly.

836821.title: About to name a mental illness or mad villain
836821.explanation: Fires on the linking word just before a psychiatric condition is named, in text about madness and diagnosis: "diagnosed with" (dementia praecox, manic-depression, paranoid schizophrenia), "suffered from" bipolar disorder, "his diagnosis was", "would today be called" schizophrenia, "predisposition toward" psychiatric problems, "committed to the state asylum for". A second, related group is Batman's insane or psychopathic criminals: it fires just before or on the label of the villain, as in "performance as" the Joker, "to stop" Two-Face, "led by" the Joker, "psychopathic nemesis", "serial killer", "mob boss ... sociopathic", and an asylum for the criminally insane "run by" Dr. Crane. It is driven by the preceding context of mental disorder or deranged criminality and anticipates the name to come; the same words ("with", "of", "as", "by") in ordinary contexts, and text about juvenile delinquency or social programmes, do not fire it.

837039.title: Capital J opening a name; hyphenated "-im"
837039.explanation: The unit reacts to the marked token itself, a short opening fragment of a longer word. The main group is a lone capital 'J' that begins a proper name still to be spelled out: Jor-El and Jax-Ur in Superman/Krypton texts, Jura and Joux in Swiss geography, Jafarov, JAB Holding; more weakly whole J-names such as Jack, Jason and Jezebel. A second, separate group is the fragment 'im' right after a hyphen or at a word start: anti-imperialist, re-implemented, 'Imma Be'. It does not depend on the topic (comics, Swiss cantons, politics and source code all appear), and the two groups share only being a word-initial letter fragment, so this is a spelling unit rather than one idea.

837126.title: First half of a name or fixed term
837126.explanation: The unit fires on a word that opens a name or set term whose second half is about to follow: most often the first name "Thomas" or a rank or title ("General", "Colonel", "Warden", "James", "Jim") just before the surname, and also the linking word or word-piece inside a fixed term ("Book of" before Mormon, "referred to as" before the quoted name, "C" before -4, "c" before ush drive, "rec" before losed, "un" before rolling). The strongest cases sit in factual prose about 18th and 19th century America (Revolutionary War officers, Latter Day Saint history) and in technical descriptions of motorcycle and gun parts ("used" Fireblade parts, "rebound", rethreading it "for" the breech-plug). It reacts to the position just before a predictable completion rather than to one word, so the pattern is loose: two or three related groups (Thomas and titles before surnames; Book of Mormon phrases; mechanical part terms) rather than a single clean idea. Ordinary first names in running story text and plain function words that do not open a known name or term do not fire it strongly.

837457.title: About to name a specific prison or lock-up
837457.explanation: The unit fires in text about people being locked up, at the small linking word that comes right before the name of a particular place of confinement: "transferred to" Wormwood Scrubs, "detainees at" Guantanamo, "prisoners in" Guantanamo Bay, "waiting on" death row, and the "HM Prison" / "HMP" / "H"-Blocks prefix just before the prison's own name (Pentonville, Wandsworth, Barlinnie, Prescoed). It is reacting to what comes next (a named jail, secure hospital or asylum is expected) rather than to the marked word itself, and British prisons are the strongest cases; in the plot summaries the same pattern appears more weakly before Arkham Asylum, Blackgate Penitentiary, "another prison" and a state hospital for the criminally insane. It does not fire on the act of imprisoning as a verb ("imprisons", "in prison" as a general state, which belong to the opposite pole), nor on the same prepositions before ordinary places.

838642.title: Naval and warship history, mid-phrase before a name
838642.explanation: The unit reacts to what the text before it is about, not to the marked token: it fires in encyclopedic prose about navies, warships, fleets, naval guns, sinkings and ports (Russo-Japanese War, Port Arthur, cruisers, submarines, torpedoed ships, register tons), in English and Russian. Within such text it peaks on a small linking word inside a noun phrase ("of", "in", "the", "to", "a", or a modifier such as "net", "flying", "requisite") just before the specific noun or proper name arrives (Port Arthur, 1st Fleet, British submarine, IMO Numbers). A few strong passages are off-topic (a legal test, a city district, aerodynamics, Ruby code), so the naval theme is dominant but not total. In ordinary film plots it fires only weakly, at a comma, slash or job title that introduces a character's name ("his partner, Robin,", "police lieutenant", "oceanographer"); the same linking words in non-technical narrative do not drive it strongly.

840061.title: Inside Malay/Indonesian names; eponymous animal names
840061.explanation: The pattern is loose. Most of the strongest firings sit inside or just before Malay and Indonesian words and proper names in English articles about Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, peaking part-way through the name with more of it still to come («Malaik-at» Tanpa Sayap, «S-inar-an» Hati, «Anuger-ah» Planet Muzik, «Pad-ang» Mengkuang, «Peg-awai» Kastam, «P-ura» Pakualaman, «at» the Kuala Lumpur airport, the opening quote before Solo). A second group is animal common names in zoology text, on the possessive «'s» or adjective just before the animal («Forsten's» cat snake, «Shortridge's» langur, «reticulate» banded gecko, moles «,» and solenodons), and a third is a capital «Q» starting an unusual name (Qiu, QVC, Qadi). Ordinary English names and ordinary possessives do not trigger it strongly; in the plot summaries it fires only weakly, on «at», «from» and commas before a place or a named person, with no clear link to the main groups.

841482.title: About to name a DC comics character
841482.explanation: Fires in text about DC superhero comics (most strongly the Flash and his circle: Barry Allen, Iris, Johnny Quick, Jay Garrick, Aquaman) on the word or comma that comes just before a named character is introduced: a linking word ("married to", "Johnny Quick and", "joined forces with", a comma in a list of heroes) or a role label ("character", "brother", "businessman", "dealer", "mastermind", "billionaire", "board member"). It reacts to the superhero setting plus the expectation that a character's name comes next, not to the marked token itself. A smaller, unrelated group is the syllable "bi" in "biotechnology", and one firing is on a digit of a 1940s issue date. The same role words and connectives in non-comics text, and mentions of comics as a medium or franchise ("Marvel Comics", "film", "series"), do not fire it; those belong to the opposite pole.

844471.title: Linking word before a venue inside a city
844471.explanation: It fires on a small linking word (in, at, as, of, within, into, including, and, 's, a comma) at the moment the text is placing something at a specific local spot inside a big city: a neighbourhood, ward, downtown core, gallery, concert hall, tavern, alley or warehouse. The context matters more than the word itself: most of the strongest passages are about Toronto (wards, neighbourhoods, venues), with Montreal and New York next, and the unit peaks just before the venue or district is named rather than on the name. In the plot summaries the same thing shows up as 'at' before a named building or function, 'into' before a warehouse, and a weaker group on 'attorney' in 'district attorney', a city office. Ordinary uses of 'in' or 'at' that are not locating something within a city's local geography do not appear.

844528.title: Just before a specific known name is completed
844528.explanation: There is no single word or topic here; the firings share only a position: the model is one step away from producing a specific name it can already anticipate. One group is a lone letter "I", "i" or "í" that begins a word or acronym still to be finished (IUPAC, IHE, Ibero-America, Iber, iambic, iudicum, íntegro, the film title "I Still Know..."). The other group is a linking or describing word right before a named person, group, work or event that the context points to ("perpetrator" before Dylann Roof, "deadly" before the Charlottesville protest, "a gang called" before the Mutants, "referred to" before "as Hush", "belonged to" before Black Mask, "and" before the League of Assassins, the comma or quote after "Mary J. Blige" before Mudbound, a digit inside a year). The same words do not fire it in ordinary places where no particular name is due, and the two groups are only loosely tied together, so this reading is tentative.

844666.title: Slot just before a specific name or term
844666.explanation: The unit fires on the token that comes right before a specific identifying name is supplied for something that has just been described in general terms; it reacts to what is about to come, not to the marked word itself. In story text this is a relationship or role word, or the comma after it, just before the person's name ("his wife" Iris, "childhood best friend," Barry Allen, "long-time friend" Booster Gold, "twin brother," Harvey, "a hostage," Marian Drews). In science and reference text it is the comma, article, hyphen, space or dash just before the exact term that completes the description ("a structural analog," deoxyribose; "xylitol is a" sugar alcohol; "the lid or" operculum; "D-iditol" 2-dehydrogenase; "Togtoh County," Inner Mongolia; a film title then "(" or "–" before the character's name). It does not fire on the name or term itself, nor on commas and articles that are not opening a naming slot.

850816.title: Just before a specific recalled proper name
850816.explanation: The unit fires at the point where the text has set up a slot that only one particular, known name can fill, and the name is about to be given or has just begun. The peak sits on the link word or role word right before the name ("Tatum and" -> Beadle, "in the early 1970s by" -> Bruce Ames, "Treaty of" -> Ouchy / Fontainebleau / Tordesillas, "his lover," -> Wallis Simpson, "his butler" / "raised by" -> Alfred Pennyworth, "Thomas and" -> Martha Wayne, "his uncle", "young son") or on the first fragment of the name itself ("O" of Otranto, Ouchy, Oricum; "Geno"; "Syn" of Synthia). Ordinary uses of "by", "of" or "and" that are not followed by a particular person, place or treaty name to be recalled do not fire it; a few weaker cases (a quoted line of statute, "National Theatre of") are the same idea of completing a fixed, memorised wording.

852645.title: Initial H of names; naming a letter/logo
852645.explanation: Most of the strongest firings are on a lone letter H (usually capital, occasionally R or T) that is the first piece of an uncommon name or technical term split into pieces: Halyomorpha, Heteronotinae, HUBCAP, Hawkman, Hama, Hemiptera, hicksii, Hush, Riddler. A second, related group is the word just before a letter, symbol or emblem is named or described by its shape: 'resembling the Latin letter W', 'denoted by the Greek letter', 'capital letters M and T', 'the iconic purple and orange colour scheme', 'commonality with the Batman logo', and in the plot summaries 'the' or 'as a' before an alias or costume (the Riddler, the masked vigilante Batman, as a disguise, as a hero). It does not fire on a lower-case h that begins an ordinary English word such as hatched, hitherto or hoods.

853515.title: Just before a Central Asian or Iranian place name
853515.explanation: The unit fires on a small linking word or comma ("of", "and", "from", "in", ",", "now") in a history text about medieval Central Asia and greater Iran, at the point where a place name of that region is about to follow: "the province of" Khwarazm, "Khurasan and" Transoxiana, "the governor of" Khurasan, "sent from" Hamadan, "home province of" Sistan, "Bukhara and" Samarkand, "Ashkhabad," Krasnovodsk. It is reacting to what comes next, not to the marked word itself: the surrounding talk of Timurids, Khwarazmians, Mongols, Sogdians, Bactria and Khurasan makes the next word a predictable regional name. The same prepositions and commas in text about other parts of the world do not fire it; the plot-summary firings are weak (under half strength) and only loosely alike, falling on a slot just before a person's name or title.

853542.title: Just before a predictable franchise name
853542.explanation: The unit fires at the point where a specific, already-determined name or word is about to be spelled out: on the small linking word in front of it ("The Return of" Chef, "Kevin Rahm as" Ted Chaough, "with" Steve, "arrest of" the Joker, "known as" Two-Face, "led by" the Joker) or on its first letter or fragment (T-antive IV, H-oth, H-osnian Prime, T-urd Burglars, Fort Garland, t-ulku). Most of the strongest cases sit inside write-ups of well-known film and television series (Star Wars, South Park, Sex and the City, Mad Men, Star Trek, Batman), where the context makes the coming character, place or episode name guessable. A weaker second group is the first letter of an ordinary word in Hindi, Russian, Portuguese or German that the sentence has made predictable. It does not fire on the finished name itself, nor on linking words that lead into open, unpredictable text.

854367.title: Cryptocurrency text; role label before a person's name
854367.explanation: The strongest firings fall into two loosely related groups, not one idea. The first is cryptocurrency and blockchain material: source code for coin clients and JSON-RPC wallets (block hash, transaction, eth_get..., coin.volume_btc) and news about bitcoin prices or token platforms, where it fires on almost any token once the topic is established. The second is ordinary prose at the moment a specific person is being named right after a role or relationship label: 'singer-songwriter Ben', 'Mayor Fletcher', 'Treasury Secretary Henry', 'governor Culbert', 'grandson of Archibald', 'forensic accountant Edward', 'Captain Ellen', 'mob boss Carl Gr-', 'her father, Commissioner'; it also fires on the first word of a book title (Blood Rites, Bloodsucking Fiends). Names that appear without such an introducing label, and code that is not about coins or blockchains, do not show up.

854726.title: Link token just before a cited source or name
854726.explanation: Fires on a small linking token (an opening bracket, a comma, "by", "from") that comes right after a work, court case, author or thing has been mentioned and right before its exact identification is supplied: a legal citation ("Mount Laurel case (", "Shumlin,", "Volpe,", "Inc.,"), a book or chapter title after an author ("Spencer,", "Pope,", "Lohner (", "comes from"), a date or foreign-language name in brackets, or the owner or designer after "owned by" / "designed by". It is reacting to what is about to come (a reference, title or proper name), not to the marked token itself; ordinary commas, brackets and "by" that do not introduce a source or name do not fire. In the plot summaries it is weaker and fires on the word just before a character's name is given ("birth of", "calling himself", "asylum doctor", "sidekick", "serial killer").

856277.title: Small linking word before an obligatory completion (mostly French)
856277.explanation: The unit reacts to a short grammatical token in the middle of a tightly bound phrase, at the point where the next word is forced: in French text, the elided pronoun "l'" or the words "à", "de", "il", "est" just before the verb they introduce ("commencent à", "décide de l'", "avant de", "il" before "y avait"). The same thing happens more weakly in English on a token that must be completed by a fixed name or noun: "New York" before "Americans", "the" or "Lions'" before "practice squad", "cap-o" before "mandamento", and in the plot summaries on a role or relation word just before a person's name ("police officer", "antiquities dealer", "dating", "relationship with"). It is about what comes next rather than the meaning of the passage; the topics are unrelated (weather code, a mafia boss, a mango article, football rosters), and the same French words at the start of a clause or after a name (the opposite pole) do not fire it. The pattern is loose, so treat it as a grammatical-position unit rather than a concept.

862924.title: About to name a place in franchise fiction
862924.explanation: Fires inside summaries of comic-book, cartoon and toy-franchise stories (Masters of the Universe, Superman, Batman, Spider-Man, The Flintstones, Tiny Toons, even Toontown game code) at the point where an in-world place, people or institution is about to be named. The peak sits on the small word just before it ("at" Slate & Company, "at" Acme Looniversity, "the" Lazarus Pit, "the" Gotham Stock Exchange, "at" Blackgate Prison, "in" the sewers, "his" lair) or on the first letter of the invented name ("E" of Eternia/Eternian, "K" of Krypton/Kryptonian). It is the franchise setting plus the coming location or name that matters, not the word itself: the same "at", "the" or "in" in ordinary prose outside such stories does not appear. Weaker cases are looser (a Lego set number, a surname after "Dr. Sam", a bracket in an anime cast list).

880592.title: Split-off letter F starting a word piece
880592.explanation: The unit fires on a small token that is just the sound "f" (often with a space, hyphen, underscore or the tail of the previous piece attached) when it opens a word or a part of a compound whose remainder is still to come: Knochen-f-unde, ant-if-aschistische, Sinter-f-ahnen, Musk-elf-asern, F-ossilien, F-landers, "F"-atty, too_f-ancy, Vegetable_f-ats, Two-F-ace, F-ries, F-earsome. The same happens in other scripts with the matching letter (Japanese フ in ファミコン, Hindi फ, Arabic ف), so it is the letter or sound and its position that count, not the meaning of the word or the subject of the text. All the examples are broken-off fragments, not complete words beginning with f, and it is not every such fragment: the opposite pole of the neuron takes the "f" of "fathoms".

881860.title: About to repeat a name already mentioned
881860.explanation: The unit fires at the point where a proper name that the document has already used is about to come back, or has just begun: on the first letter of "Columbia" after a long run of "(Columbia, 1959)" entries, on "in" before "Columbia County", on "at" before "Columbia", on "from" before "Team RBM", on a comma before "Russell" or "Chelsea", on the first letter of "Jupiter" and "Gemonensis". It reacts to what comes next, not to the marked token itself, which is usually a small word (in, at, from, by, on, between, the), a comma, a line break or an opening bracket. "Columbia" is by far the most frequent name, with Hamilton, Russell, Chelsea, Brooklyn and New York also recurring, and in the plot summaries it fires just before an established character or place is named again ("invited by" Bruce, "assault on" Batman, "between" Robin and Batman). The same small words do not fire it when a new, not yet mentioned name or an ordinary noun follows.

881889.title: Opening fragment of an unfinished name or word
881889.explanation: The unit fires on the first piece of a word that the tokenizer has split, at the moment the word has begun but is not yet finished: " W" of Wapiti, " Con" of Conopomorpha, " Tor" of Torrens, " Al" of Al Mansurah, "Acid" of Acidalia, "Are" of Arendelle, " reve" of a misspelt "reveales", "unve" of unveils, "im" of imprisoned. Most are proper names, titles, Latin species names or uncommon words whose ending can be supplied from the context just before (the maker of the aircraft, the singer of the song, the common name of the animal), and the same holds for the first character of Japanese and Chinese compounds. A few weaker cases are whole short words that open a known title or verse line ("The" Penguin Guide, rainbow "of"). It reacts to the position in the word, not to any topic, and it does not fire on complete ordinary words or on the later pieces that finish a word.
